author: Bonizo Placentinus
title: Fragmentum historiae pontificiae (Bonizo Placentinus)
summary: In a catalogue of Gregory the Great's works, Bonizo notes that the Moralia in Job treats Job morally, allegorically and historically; the senses are named in passing only.

author: Bruno Carthusianorum
title: Expositio in Psalmos (Bruno Carthusianorum)
senses_latin: intellectus ad litteram > mysticus intellectus > anagoge
example_figure: pennae columbae deargentatae et posteriora dorsi in pallore auri
definitions: intellectus ad litteram: literal understanding, bright like silver | mysticus intellectus: mystical understanding, called anagoge by the Greeks, signified by pale gold, far more perfect than the literal
summary: Expounding Ps 67:14, Bruno reads the dove's silvered wings as the literal understanding and the pale gold as the mystical understanding (Greek anagoge), more perfect than the letter; worthy church leaders abound in both.

author: Guigo II prior Carthusiae
title: De quadripertito exercitio cellae (Guigo II prior Carthusiae)
summary: In advising the cell-dweller to meditate on all the books of scripture and the doctors, Guigo names in passing the four ways things are rightly understood: historically, allegorically, tropologically or anagogically, without defining or applying them.

author: Radulfus Ardens
title: Homiliae (Radulfus Ardens)
summary: Homily on the Canaanite woman announcing a threefold reading (letter, allegory, tropology), then beginning the literal reading: her faith, fervour, perseverance and humility are commended.

author: Radulfus Ardens
title: Homiliae (Radulfus Ardens)
summary: Homily on the feeding of the five thousand announces a threefold treatment: literal, tropological, then mystical. It begins the literal reading, where Christ shows true humanity in compassion and true divinity in the miracle of the loaves.

author: Radulfus Ardens
title: Homiliae (Radulfus Ardens)
definitions: historia: exterior sense that feeds the unlearned | moralitas: grouped with history as an exterior sense nourishing the simple | allegoria: interior sense that exercises the wise
summary: Commenting on the disciples' 'now you speak plainly', the homily warns against reading only Scripture's surface. Scripture is tempered so the little one walks and the giant swims: exterior history or morality feeds the simple, interior allegory exercises the wise.

author: Radulfus Ardens
title: Homiliae (Radulfus Ardens)
senses_latin: littera > intellectus spiritualis > historialiter > mystice > tropologice > anagogice
example_figure: Littera occidit, spiritus vivificat; gladium emere (Luc. 22)
definitions: sensus litterae: outward, surface sense of the words; the 'flesh' that profits nothing | intellectus spiritualis: inward understanding of scripture
summary: Glossing 2 Cor 3:6, sets the outward surface letter, which misled Jews and heretics, against the inward spiritual understanding. Figures, moral precepts and some New Testament sayings taken only literally kill. Ministers must discern what is said historically, mystically, tropologically, anagogically.

author: Guibertus S. Mariae de Novigento
title: Moralia in Genesin (Guibertus S. Mariae de Novigento)
definitions: historia: speaks of things that were done | allegoria: one thing is understood from another | tropologia: moral speech, treating the composing and ordering of morals | anagoge: spiritual understanding leading upward to highest, heavenly things
summary: Four rules of Scripture, wheels on which the sacred page turns: history, allegory, tropology, anagogy, defined and illustrated by Jerusalem. For preaching, the moral sense is most useful; allegory builds faith but risks error for the unlearned.

author: Guibertus S. Mariae de Novigento
title: Tropologiae in prophetas Osee et Amos ac Lamentationes Jeremiae (Guibertus S. Mariae de Novigento)
definitions: anagoge: the higher understanding drawn from scripture that pertains to the contemplation of God
summary: Expounding Hosea 9:2, Guibert makes the threshing floor the divine books, which yield the fruits of allegory and tropology (moral knowledge). The winepress is those who press out anagoge, the understanding that leads to contemplation of God.

author: Wernerus S. Blasii
title: Libri deflorationum (Wernerus S. Blasii)
summary: A mystical reading of the Magi story. The three gifts offered from the opened treasures (skill in letters) are glossed as physics, logic and ethics, or as history, allegory and tropology, or as faith in the Trinity. The senses are named, not defined.

author: Wernerus S. Blasii
title: Libri deflorationum (Wernerus S. Blasii)
example_figure: architriclinus; hydriae at the wedding of Cana
summary: An allegorical exposition of the Cana miracle. In passing, it identifies the steward as one skilled in Scripture, which contains histories, moralities and allegories. Those learned in the law 'according to the letter' receive the Gospel without knowing its source.

author: Wernerus S. Blasii
title: Libri deflorationum (Wernerus S. Blasii)
definitions: historia: text taken just as the letter narrates it | allegoria: one thing is said, another understood | moralitas: morals are instructed through what is read | anagoge: higher sense, teaching heavenly and eternal things
summary: Wisdom's table (Prov 9) stands on four feet because Scripture is understood in four ways: history, allegory, morality and anagoge, each briefly defined. The seven pillars are seven sapiential books painted by Gregory and Augustine.

author: Eadmerus Cantuariensis
title: De S. Anselmi similitudinibus (Eadmerus Cantuariensis)
definitions: historia: the simple deeds and examples of the saints | allegoria: instruction in the faith | moralitas: ordering of morals, by which we compose our conduct | anagoge: understanding tending upward; contemplation; sweetest affection of divine love uniting soul to God
summary: Scripture is the king's wine-cellar holding four casks: simple history, allegory, morality, and anagoge (contemplation), each sweeter than the last. They are poured according to the reader's capacity. Faith is the cellar's door and humility its key.

author: Eadmerus Cantuariensis
title: De S. Anselmi similitudinibus (Eadmerus Cantuariensis)
example_figure: cellarium Domini et dolia (the Lord's wine cellar and its casks)
definitions: anagoge: the last cask, holding the wine that gladdens the heart; unreachable without faith
summary: Scripture is the Lord's wine cellar. Its door is faith and its key humility. Its casks are history, allegory, morality and contemplation. Secular learning may lick drops from the first casks, but only the faithful and humble reach the last, anagoge.

author: Berengosus Trevirensis
title: De laude et inventione sanctae crucis (Berengosus Trevirensis)
summary: Having expounded Naaman's name morally (as the gentile people), the author turns to Constantine's name; since it cannot be read allegorically, he explains it historically by etymological derivation from Constans and Constantius.

author: Berengosus Trevirensis
title: De mysterio ligni Dominici (Berengosus Trevirensis)
senses_latin: typice > moraliter > mysticus > allegorice > historice > spiritalis intelligentia > allegoricus
summary: After reading the thau of Ezekiel typically as the cross, the author says the number one hundred has been treated morally. Fifty must first be computed 'historically' (ten times five) before its many spiritual meanings are treated allegorically, in part.

author: Sigebertus Gemblacensis
title: De scriptoribus ecclesiasticis (Sigebertus Gemblacensis)
summary: In a catalogue entry on Gregory the Great, Sigebert notes that Gregory, at Leander's request, expounded Job threefold, historically, allegorically and morally, in the Moralia (35 books). This is a passing bibliographic mention only.

author: Anselmus Laudunensis
title: Ennarrationes in Matthaeum (Anselmus Laudunensis)
definitions: allegoria: how each ancestor in the genealogy prefigures Christ | moralitas: some virtue built up in us from each father, through his name's meaning or his example
summary: For Matthew's genealogy, three things are to be noted in each father: history; allegory, how he prefigures Christ; and morality, a virtue built in us by his name or example. The 42 fathers parallel Israel's 42 stations.

author: Anselmus Laudunensis
title: Ennarrationes in Matthaeum (Anselmus Laudunensis)
example_figure: Abraham genuit Isaac (Abraham fides, Isaac spes)
summary: On the Matthean genealogy: the history (Abraham begat Isaac, etc.) is not in doubt, so the commentator turns to moral and allegorical readings, beginning the moral: Abraham signifies faith, Isaac hope, since faith begets hope.

author: Auctor incertus (Guillelmus de Campellis?)
title: Dialogus inter Christianum et Judaeum (Auctor incertus (Guillelmus de Campellis?))
senses_latin: historia > littera > allegorice > moraliter > figuraliter > litteraliter
summary: The Christian argues that Ps 132:3 (dew of Hermon descending on Sion) is impossible literally and must be read allegorically: grace descends from the Lord onto contemplative souls. Some texts are read allegorically, some morally, some literally; the old law spoke figuratively (nut and shell).

author: Hildebertus Cenomanensis
title: Sermones (Hildebertus Cenomanensis)
example_figure: porta (limen, liminaria, limes); quatuor pedes mensae Domini
definitions: historia: the threshold underlying the other senses, contained in God's three works: creation, reconciliation, confirmation
summary: Scripture is compared to a door with four parts (threshold, two side-posts, lintel) and to the four feet of the Lord's table: history, allegory, morality, anagoge. History is the threshold beneath the others, resting on God's threefold work.

author: Hildebertus Cenomanensis
title: Sermones (Hildebertus Cenomanensis)
summary: Sacred reading, one of the monk's four occupations, is a four-legged table in God's house with history, allegory, tropology and anagogy. Each sense is illustrated by a different verse naming Jerusalem.

author: Hildebertus Cenomanensis
title: Sermones (Hildebertus Cenomanensis)
definitions: moralitas: the moral sense, yielding precepts of modesty, teachings of true religion, examples of holy living
summary: Exhorting pastors to preach, Hildebert says Scripture offers varied flowers: the simplicity of histories, the mysteries of allegories, and the sweetness of morality. The moral sense supplies precepts and examples, and preachers must ruminate on Scripture with discretion.

author: Hildebertus Cenomanensis
title: Sermones (Hildebertus Cenomanensis)
summary: Scripture is likened to the wine-cellar where we are refreshed by manifold understanding. Whether we seek moral teaching, allegorical understanding, historical truth or anagogical revelation, we find it all there, the storehouse of the Holy Spirit.

author: Gaufridus Grossus
title: Vita B. Bernardi (Gaufridus Grossus)
summary: Allegorizing the ass's jawbone as the preacher, the passage says he must chew scripture finely, keeping historical, allegorical, tropological and anagogical understanding distinct, then pass it to simple folk through all these modes.

author: Honorius Augustodunensis
title: De exsilio et patria animae (Honorius Augustodunensis)
senses_latin: historicus > allegoricus > tropologicus > anagogicus > historia > allegoria > tropologia > moralitas > anagoge
definitions: historia: a thing done, an event that happened | allegoria: one thing is said, another is understood | tropologia: moral meaning | anagoge: higher sense leading to God and the world to come
summary: Scripture, the soul's homeland after the liberal arts, is a house of Wisdom on seven pillars whose four walls are the historical, allegorical, tropological and anagogical senses. Each is defined and illustrated by Jerusalem: Jewish city, Church, faithful soul, heavenly city.

author: Honorius Augustodunensis
title: Expositio in Cantica canticorum (Honorius Augustodunensis)
senses_latin: historice > allegorice > tropologice > anagogice > historia > allegoria > tropologia > anagoge
example_figure: nuptiae (sponsus et sponsa, Christus et Ecclesia)
definitions: historia: literal marriage, by bodily union or by betrothal alone (Mary and Joseph; Solomon and Pharaoh's daughter) | allegoria: the Word joining human flesh to itself; Christ uniting the whole Church to himself | tropologia: the soul joined to Christ by love; the lower soul joined to the spirit by consenting to divine law
summary: In the accessus to the Song, Honorius says the book treats marriage in four modes (historical, allegorical, tropological, anagogical), each realized in two ways, and defines each. The excerpt breaks off at anagoge.

author: Honorius Augustodunensis
title: Expositio in Cantica canticorum (Honorius Augustodunensis)
senses_latin: historice > allegorice > tropologice > anagogice > historia > allegoria > tropologia > anagoge > historicus > allegoricus > tropologicus > anagogicus
definitions: historia: the event narrated as it happened | allegoria: the thing expounded of Christ and the Church | tropologia: referred to the soul and spirit | anagoge: understood of the life above | historia: the thing noted as it was done | allegoria: the interpretation of names is considered | tropologia: a comparison drawn from deeds done is investigated | anagoge: the likeness of things is weighed
summary: Scripture is understood in four ways (historical, allegorical, tropological, anagogical). These are figured by the four-legged showbread table and Ezekiel's four-faced wheel, defined twice, illustrated by Solomon's temple, then applied to Song 1:1.

author: Honorius Augustodunensis
title: Expositio in Cantica canticorum (Honorius Augustodunensis)
summary: Expounding Solomon's litter as the table of Scripture, Honorius reads its pillars (feet) as the four senses—history, allegory, tropology, anagogy—silver because Scripture shines with eloquence. He names them without defining them.

author: Honorius Augustodunensis
title: Expositio in Cantica canticorum (Honorius Augustodunensis)
summary: Commenting on the praise of the bride in the Song, Honorius remarks that here the historical sense fails, just as allegory, tropology or anagogy sometimes do not run through every detail. Not every verse bears all four senses.

author: Honorius Augustodunensis
title: Expositio in Cantica canticorum (Honorius Augustodunensis)
example_figure: sponsa dormiens, cor vigilans; vox dilecti pulsantis
summary: On the bride's lament (Song 5): the passage is assigned more to tropology than allegory, since the Church exhorts penitents to good morals, so allegory lapses here; anagogically the pilgrim Church sleeps to earthly things, is called heavenward through death.

author: Honorius Augustodunensis
title: Expositio in Cantica canticorum (Honorius Augustodunensis)
summary: Honorius remarks that this chapter of the Song lacks the historical and anagogical senses but shines with allegory and tropology, because it concerns only Christ and his members. He then expounds the beloved, white and ruddy.

author: Honorius Augustodunensis
title: Gemma animae (Honorius Augustodunensis)
example_figure: quatuor lectiones Sabbati sancti (diluvium, mare Rubrum, septem mulieres)
summary: The four Holy Saturday readings correspond to four kinds of faithful (simple, understanding, advanced, wise), who are taught through four senses: history, allegory, tropology, anagogy. The senses are named, not defined, and are set within liturgical allegory.

author: Honorius Augustodunensis
title: Gemma animae (Honorius Augustodunensis)
definitions: historia: narrates things done | allegoria: through a thing done indicates something else | tropologia: instructs morals | anagoge: leads the understanding to higher things
summary: The four-legged table of the tabernacle signifies Scripture with four senses, defined in turn. The four Holy Saturday lessons (Gen 1, Exod 14, Isa 4...) then instruct the simple, the intelligent and the advanced by history, allegory and tropology respectively.

author: Honorius Augustodunensis
title: Gemma animae (Honorius Augustodunensis)
example_figure: four lessons of the Pentecost vigil (Gen 22, Deut 32, Isa 4, Baruch 3)
summary: Honorius assigns one sense to each of the four vigil lessons: Genesis 22 sounds history; Deuteronomy 32 the new law, followed by an allegorical canticle; Isaiah 4:1 (seven women, seven gifts) tropology, giving morals; Baruch 3 anagogy, eternal joy.

author: Honorius Augustodunensis
title: Sacramentarium (Honorius Augustodunensis)
senses_latin: historicus > allegoricus > tropologicus > moralis > anagogicus > superior > historia > allegoria > tropologia
definitions: historia: the event is related just as it happened | allegoria: mystical words or things signify Christ's presence and the Church's sacraments | tropologia: moral speech for forming conduct, in plain or figurative words
summary: The four Holy Saturday vigil lessons for catechumens correspond to the four feet of the tabernacle table, i.e. the four senses of Scripture. History, allegory and tropology are defined and exemplified by Genesis 1, Exodus 14 and Isaiah 4. The excerpt breaks off before anagogy is defined.

author: Honorius Augustodunensis
title: Speculum ecclesiae (Honorius Augustodunensis)
definitions: hystoria: the text taken just as the letter narrates it | allegoria: one thing is said, another understood | moralitas: morals are formed through what is read | anagoge: the higher sense, teaching heavenly and eternal things
summary: Wisdom's table (Prov. 9) rests on four feet because Scripture is understood in four ways: history (as the letter narrates), allegory (saying one thing, meaning another), morality (forming conduct), and anagoge (the higher sense teaching heavenly, eternal things).

author: Auctor incertus (Hugo de S. Victore?)
title: Posteriores excerptiones (Auctor incertus (Hugo de S. Victore?))
example_figure: ager Jacob (sacra Scriptura), pastores, greges, puteus, lapis
summary: Within an allegory of Jacob's journey, the field is Scripture and its shepherds are teachers. Different flocks (married, continent, virgins) are fed some by history, some by allegory, some by tropology. The stone on the well is the difficulty of understanding.

author: Auctor incertus (Hugo de S. Victore?)
title: Posteriores excerptiones (Auctor incertus (Hugo de S. Victore?))
summary: In allegorizing the table of showbread as Scripture, the four supports of the table are said to be the four senses of Scripture (history, allegory, tropology, anagoge), by which Scripture is raised up from earthly things.

author: Auctor incertus (Hugo de S. Victore?)
title: Posteriores excerptiones (Auctor incertus (Hugo de S. Victore?))
summary: In an allegorical reading of the furnishings of Elisha's upper room, the table signifies Scripture. Like a table full of food, Scripture gives one refreshment through history, another through allegory, another through tropology, and likewise through the Old and New Testaments.

author: Hugo de S. Victore
title: Adnotatiunculae in Joelem (Hugo de S. Victore)
summary: Commenting on Joel 2:18, Hugh reads 'terra' historically as the synagogue (earthly desire), allegorically as the Church (stability of faith), morally as the faithful soul (humility and abstinence).

author: Hugo de S. Victore
title: De scripturis et scriptoribus sacris (Hugo de S. Victore)
senses_latin: historia > allegoria > allegoria simplex > anagoge > littera > spiritualis
definitions: historia: Strictly, things seen and narrated; broadly, the first sense from words signifying things | allegoria: What the letter signifies points to another deed, past, present or future; 'other-speaking' | allegoria simplex: A visible deed signifies another invisible deed | anagoge: Upward leading; through the visible an invisible deed is declared
summary: Hugh sets out a threefold exposition: history (from historeo, broadly the first verbal sense), and allegory, subdivided into simple allegory and anagoge. He illustrates with Job on the dunghill as Christ, and as the penitent soul (what ought to be done).

author: Hugo de S. Victore
title: De scripturis et scriptoribus sacris (Hugo de S. Victore)
senses_latin: historia > allegoria > littera > spiritualis > tropologia > mores > mystica
definitions: allegoria: things signified by words signify further things; one deed signifies another deed | tropologia: what the deed signifies as to be done, i.e. worth doing | sacramentum: literal deeds that represent spiritual realities
summary: Reads Job on the dunghill: historically plain, allegorically Christ humbled in the world, morally the penitent soul. Then argues that not every text bears the threefold sense; like a cithara's frame, some parts are only literal, moral or spiritual.

author: Hugo de S. Victore
title: De scripturis et scriptoribus sacris (Hugo de S. Victore)
senses_latin: historia > allegoria > tropologia > spiritualiter > mores > interpretatio litteralis > historica > mystica intelligentia > littera
definitions: mystica intelligentia: spiritual understanding gathered only from what the letter first sets forth | littera: expounding the letter is showing what the letter signifies
summary: Not every passage bears all three senses (history, allegory, tropology). Like a harp's strings and frame, some texts are only spiritual, some moral, some literal. The literal sense is necessary. He rebukes allegorists who ignore the letter. Lion/Christ: things, not words, signify.

author: Hugo de S. Victore
title: De scripturis et scriptoribus sacris (Hugo de S. Victore)
summary: Divine reading bears a twofold fruit, knowledge and moral instruction. Knowledge pertains more to history and allegory, moral instruction more to tropology. The liberal arts serve this knowledge, the trivium for the signification of words and the quadrivium for the signification of things.

author: Hugo de S. Victore
title: Expositio in Abdiam (Hugo de S. Victore)
summary: Preface to Obadiah: simple in words, manifold in sense. Literally the prophecy is aimed at Idumaea, allegorically against the world, tropologically against the flesh. Obadiah bears the type of the Saviour, whose coming destroys the world and subdues the flesh.

author: Hugo de S. Victore
title: Expositio in Abdiam (Hugo de S. Victore)
senses_latin: historia > allegoria > tropologia > historialiter > allegorice > tropologice
summary: Hugh reads Obadiah 8-9 under three senses. Historically, destruction is threatened against the Idumaean people. Allegorically, it falls on heretics or gentiles. Tropologically, it falls on the flesh. 'That day' is the Babylonian advent, Christ's advent in the flesh, and his advent into the mind.

author: Hugo de S. Victore
title: Expositio in Abdiam (Hugo de S. Victore)
summary: Reads Obadiah's verses in three senses in turn. Historically, the Babylonians destroy Edom for wronging Israel. Allegorically, Christ calls the gentiles and heretics perish for attacking the Church. Tropologically, Christ enters the mind and the rebellious flesh is destroyed.

author: Hugo de S. Victore
title: Expositio in Abdiam (Hugo de S. Victore)
example_figure: dies peregrinationis; Hierusalem et portae ejus
summary: Reads Obadiah's verses in turn: Jerusalem's gates allegorically as the Church's prelates, tropologically as the flesh rebelling against the soul. 'Day of his estrangement' is historically captivity, allegorically present life, tropologically the heat of temptation.

author: Hugo de S. Victore
title: Expositio in Abdiam (Hugo de S. Victore)
summary: Reads Obadiah 16 threefold: historically the prophecy targets the Edomites, allegorically idolaters and heretics, tropologically the flesh and its desires; the mountain is earthly Jerusalem, Christ and the Church, and holy contemplation.

author: Hugo de S. Victore
title: Expositio in Abdiam (Hugo de S. Victore)
senses_latin: historia > prophetia > mysticus intellectus > allegorice > tropologice
summary: The prophecy against Edom was fulfilled historically under Zerubbabel. By prophecy and mystical understanding it is fulfilled daily in the Church and in each soul against the flesh. Mount Sion is allegorically the Church, tropologically the contemplative soul raised to heavenly things.

author: Hugo de Folieto
title: De claustro animae (Hugo de Folieto)
definitions: historialiter: the literal battle between Goliath and David | mystice: the battle between Christ and the devil | moraliter: the battle between any just man and a member of the devil
summary: Reads David's fight with Goliath in three ways: historically (David vs Goliath), mystically (Christ vs devil), morally (the just man vs a member of the devil). It happened in fact, occurred in mystery, and continues now in morals.

author: Hugo de S. Victore
title: De arca Noe morali (Hugo de S. Victore)
definitions: historia: the literal account, which covers the mystical meanings beneath the veil of the letter | allegoria: learning Scripture's mysteries, by which the illumined mind reaches knowledge of the divinity
summary: The seraph's three pairs of wings signify Scripture's three senses: history, allegory and tropology. Each is doubled because it kindles love of God and neighbour. History veils the mystical sense; allegory reaches toward God's incomprehensible eternity.

author: Hugo de S. Victore
title: De arca Noe morali (Hugo de S. Victore)
definitions: historia: measures the ark's length: the order of time found in the sequence of deeds done | allegoria: measures the ark's breadth: gathering of faithful peoples through sharing the sacraments | tropologia: measures the ark's height: dignity of merits grows through progress in virtues
summary: Hugh maps the three dimensions of Noah's ark onto three senses containing all Scripture: history (length, temporal order), allegory (breadth, sacramental gathering of peoples), tropology (height, growth in virtue).

author: Hugo de S. Victore
title: De arca Noe mystica (Hugo de S. Victore)
summary: In describing the ark diagram, each of the thirty scripture books on the ladders is divided externally into three steps because of the threefold understanding: history, allegory, tropology. The scheme is named in passing, not defined or applied.

author: Hugo de S. Victore
title: De arca Noe mystica (Hugo de S. Victore)
summary: In the instructions for drawing the ark diagram, Hugh assigns colours to the senses: green for history, saffron for tropology, blue for allegory. He then turns to a moral reading of the ladders, loosely called their allegory, as virtues.

author: Hugo de S. Victore
title: De artificio meditandi (Hugo de S. Victore)
definitions: historia: seeking or admiring the reason of past deeds, fitly accomplished in their times, places and manner | allegoria: attends to how preceding events signify future ones, providentially fitted to form faith | tropologia: asks what fruit the words bear: what to do and what to avoid
summary: Hugh says meditation in reading involves threefold consideration: history (reasons of past deeds, divine judgments), allegory (past events signifying future, building faith), and tropology (moral fruit: what to do, avoid, virtue, affection).

author: Hugo de S. Victore
title: De sacramentis (Hugo de S. Victore)
definitions: historia: narration of things done, contained in the first signification of the letter | allegoria: what is said to be done signifies some other deed, past, present or future | tropologia: what is said to be done signifies something that ought to be done
summary: Hugh states that Scripture treats its matter (creation, fall, restoration) under a threefold understanding—history, allegory, tropology—defines each, and argues Scripture excels because not only words but things signify.

author: Hugo de S. Victore
title: De sacramentis (Hugo de S. Victore)
definitions: historia: sense lying in the signification of words to things | allegoria: sense in which things signify mystical deeds done; forms right faith | tropologia: sense in which things signify mystical deeds to be done; forms good works
summary: Hugh defines a threefold sense: history (words signifying things), served by the trivium; allegory (things signifying mystical deeds done, forming faith) and tropology (things signifying deeds to be done, forming good works), served by the quadrivium and physics.

author: Hugo de S. Victore
title: De vanitate mundi (Hugo de S. Victore)
definitions: historia: concerns deeds done; the ark's length | allegoria: concerns the sacraments (mysteries); the ark's breadth | tropologia: concerns the virtues; the ark's height
summary: Hugh maps the ark's three dimensions onto Scripture's senses: length to deeds (history), breadth to sacraments (allegory), height to virtues (tropology), saying all divine Scripture is enclosed within these bounds; he refers to his fuller De arca.

author: Hugo de S. Victore
title: Eruditio didascalica (Hugo de S. Victore)
senses_latin: historia > allegoria > tropologia > spiritualiter > mores > historice > allegorice > tropologice
example_figure: cithara (strings and body of the lyre)
summary: Scripture has a threefold mode of understanding: history, allegory, tropology. Not every passage carries all three. Like a lyre's strings and frame, some parts are only spiritual, some moral, some simply historical, and some admit all three.

author: Hugo de S. Victore
title: Eruditio didascalica (Hugo de S. Victore)
senses_latin: historia > allegoria > tropologia > spiritualiter > mos > sensus historiae > historice > allegorice > tropologice > littera > mysticum
definitions: allegoria: insinuates something mystical beyond the historical truth | tropologia: shows what is to be done
summary: Hugh argues that not every passage bears all three senses (history, allegory, tropology). Like a harp's strings and wooden body, some parts carry only spiritual, moral or historical meaning. Assign each sense where reason demands, though sometimes one letter holds all.

author: Hugo de S. Victore
title: Eruditio didascalica (Hugo de S. Victore)
senses_latin: historia > allegoria > tropologia > spiritualis intelligentia > littera > mysticum
example_figure: cithara: chordae et lignum concavum; mel in favo
definitions: allegoria: insinuates something mystical beyond the historical truth | tropologia: shows what ought to be done
summary: Hugh compares Scripture to a lyre: spiritual sense as strings, history and letter as sounding wood. Not every passage bears history, allegory and tropology; each should be assigned where reason demands, though one letter may carry all three. He then turns to things signifying.

author: Hugo de S. Victore
title: Eruditio didascalica (Hugo de S. Victore)
definitions: historia: together with allegory, serves the knowledge that instructs the mind | allegoria: together with history, serves the knowledge that instructs the mind | tropologia: serves moral formation, adorning the mind with good conduct
summary: Divine reading has a twofold fruit: knowledge, which pertains mainly to history and allegory, and moral formation, which pertains to tropology. Hugh then begins advising the reader who seeks morality, citing Matt 6:33.

author: Hugo de S. Victore
title: Eruditio didascalica (Hugo de S. Victore)
senses_latin: historia > allegoria > tropologia > moralitas > littera > sensus > sententia
summary: Chapter list of Didascalicon Book VI: chapters on historia, allegoria, tropologia/moralitas, then on the order of exposition by littera, sensus, sententia. The senses are named as chapter headings only, not defined or applied.

author: Hugo de S. Victore
title: Eruditio didascalica (Hugo de S. Victore)
definitions: historia: the truth of past deeds: what was done, by whom, and where, learned from beginning to end
summary: Hugh sets the order of study among history, allegory and tropology with a building image: foundation first, then structure, then colour. History, covering person, deed, time and place, comes first. No one becomes subtle in allegory without grounding in history.

author: Hugo de S. Victore
title: Eruditio didascalica (Hugo de S. Victore)
senses_latin: littera > mysticus > historia > allegoria > typicus > moralitas
definitions: historia: foundation of sacred doctrine; where we marvel at God's deeds | allegoria: truth drawn from history like honey from comb; where we believe God's sacraments | moralitas: the colour painted over the building; where we imitate God's perfection
summary: Hugh's building metaphor: history is the foundation, from which allegory's truth is pressed like honey. Typical signification raises the structure of faith, and morality paints it. He then urges reading the sacred history in order, from Creation onward.

author: Auctor incertus (Hugo de S. Victore?)
title: Miscellanea (Auctor incertus (Hugo de S. Victore?))
definitions: historia: together with allegory, serves the study of knowing truth | allegoria: together with history, serves the study of knowing truth | tropologia: serves the form of virtue; twofold: plain moral instruction and affective exhortation
summary: All scripture seeks either knowledge of truth or the form of virtue. History and allegory serve the first, tropology the second. Tropology is itself twofold: plain narration that instructs morals, and affective exhortation that kindles desire for virtue.

author: Auctor incertus (Hugo de S. Victore?)
title: Miscellanea (Auctor incertus (Hugo de S. Victore?))
summary: Under a title on the fourfold sense, the name Jerusalem (Ps 121) is read four ways: historically the earthly city, allegorically the Church, tropologically each faithful soul, anagogically eternal bliss. Each sense gets a proof text, then the heavenly city is expounded.

author: Auctor incertus (Hugo de S. Victore?)
title: Miscellanea (Auctor incertus (Hugo de S. Victore?))
summary: Taking 'Laetare, Jerusalem', the passage says Jerusalem is meant in four ways. Historically it is the city on Sion; allegorically the Church founded on Christ; morally the contemplative faithful soul; anagogically the heavenly court of angels. Each rejoices accordingly.

author: Auctor incertus (Robertus Paululus?)
title: De officiis ecclesiasticis (Auctor incertus (Robertus Paululus?))
senses_latin: historicus > allegoricus > moralis > anagogicus > historia > allegoria > spiritualiter
summary: The four legs of the tabernacle table are the four expositions of Scripture (historical, allegorical, moral, anagogical). The four Easter-vigil lessons are matched to them: creation (history), the Exodus (allegory), and Isaiah's seven women (moral).

author: Auctor incertus
title: Excerptiones allegoricae (Auctor incertus)
summary: Prologue outlining the work's plan: part one covers arts, geography and the course of history; part two treats allegorical and tropological senses arranged along the underlying line of history, with books on the mysteries of events.

author: Auctor incertus
title: Excerptiones allegoricae (Auctor incertus)
definitions: historia: narration of things done, contained in the first signification of the letter | allegoria: when a deed narrated signifies another deed, past, present or future | tropologia: when from what was done we learn what we ought to do
summary: Chapter heading states that scripture treats its matter in three ways (history, allegory, tropology), defines each, and argues that scripture excels secular learning because things as well as words signify, so knowledge of things is needed.

author: Auctor incertus
title: Excerptiones allegoricae (Auctor incertus)
definitions: historia: the sense lying between words and the things they signify | allegoria: the sense between things and mystical deeds already done | tropologia: the sense between things and mystical deeds yet to be done
summary: Defines history, allegory and tropology by the relations of words to things and things to mystical deeds done or to be done. The trivium serves history; the quadrivium and physics serve allegory and tropology. Things signify by their properties.

author: Auctor incertus
title: Excerptiones allegoricae (Auctor incertus)
summary: After distinguishing four works of God, the author recalls that Scripture treats its matter, the work of restoration, threefold: history, allegory, tropology. He promises to give the historical narrative first, then expound allegory and tropology.

author: Auctor incertus
title: Sermones (Auctor incertus)
summary: In a sermon on fear of the Lord surpassing learning, the preacher lists scriptural expertise in history, allegory, tropology, anagogy (like Jerome), and moral exposition (like Gregory) among accomplishments that would make a man 'great'; no definitions.

author: Auctor incertus
title: Sermones (Auctor incertus)
example_figure: diaeta (Scripture as the diet of the sick soul)
summary: In a medical allegory of salvation, Scripture is the diet served to the sick soul in varied ways according to hearers' capacity: now by history, allegory, tropology or anagogy, now by Old or New Testament authority, veiled or plain.

author: Auctor incertus
title: Sermones (Auctor incertus)
senses_latin: sensus tropologicus > historia > allegoria > tropologia > anagoge
summary: Sermon heading reads Jerusalem fourfold: historically the earthly city, allegorically the Church, tropologically the spiritual life, anagogically the heavenly homeland. It then sets the others aside to develop the tropological sense, with walls, streets and virtues opposed to Babylon's vices.

author: Auctor incertus
title: Sermones (Auctor incertus)
summary: Allegorizing the Shunammite's furnishings for Elisha, the table signifies Scripture, which feeds us variously through history, allegory, tropology, and through the Old and New Testaments; the senses are named in passing.

author: Auctor incertus
title: Sermones (Auctor incertus)
definitions: historia: plain narration of how a thing was literally done or said | allegoria: mystical words or things signify Christ's presence and the Church's sacraments | tropologia: moral speech aimed at correcting and forming conduct, in plain or figurative words | anagoge: speech leading upward, treating future rewards and heavenly life
summary: The four feet of the tabernacle table signify the four senses of Scripture (history, allegory, tropology, anagogy), each defined with examples (Exodus lamb, Isa 11, 1 John 3, Eccl 9, Matt 5, Apoc 22); the four rings are the Gospels supporting them.

author: Auctor incertus
title: Speculum de mysteriis ecclesiae (Auctor incertus)
example_figure: quadrigae Aminadab; Jerusalem (civitas terrena, Ecclesia, fidelis anima, superna patria)
summary: In a liturgical commentary on Nocturns, the monks' four lessons signify the fourfold sense of Scripture (the chariots of Aminadab): historical, allegorical, tropological, anagogical. Jerusalem illustrates them as earthly city, Church, faithful soul and heavenly homeland.

author: Auctor incertus
title: Speculum de mysteriis ecclesiae (Auctor incertus)
senses_latin: historialis > allegoricus > moralis > historia > allegoria > tropologia > anagoge
definitions: historia: the signification of words to things; narrating deeds by words' first meaning | allegoria: one deed understood through another deed, via things not words | anagoge: upward leading; allegory whose referent is invisible and heavenly | tropologia: turning speech: from a deed is shown what ought to be done, for morals
summary: Scripture has a threefold sense because both words and things signify: history from words; allegory and tropology from things, with anagoge as heavenly allegory. Not all senses everywhere. Illustrated by Red Sea, first-day light, Jerusalem.

author: Herveus Burgidolensis
title: Commentaria in epistolas Pauli (Herveus Burgidolensis)
example_figure: Gen.2.24 duo in carne una: conjugium Christi et Ecclesiae
summary: Commenting on Ephesians 5:32, Paul is made to say that he interprets Genesis' 'two in one flesh' allegorically of Christ and the Church. His hearers should take it morally and literally: each man loves his wife as himself.

author: Zacharias Chrysopolitanus
title: De concordia evangelistarum (Zacharias Chrysopolitanus)
summary: A mystical reading of the magi (Matt 2), drawn from Hilary, says the three gifts offered from opened treasuries of learning are physics, logic and ethics, or history, allegory and tropology, or faith in the Trinity.

author: Zacharias Chrysopolitanus
title: De concordia evangelistarum (Zacharias Chrysopolitanus)
summary: Allegorical reading of the Cana wedding, drawn from Alcuin. The steward stands for leaders skilled in Scripture, which contains histories, moralities and allegories. Later, those versed in the law 'according to the letter'. The senses are named in passing only.

author: Hugo Rothomagensis
title: Dialogi (Hugo Rothomagensis)
summary: Within a moral-spiritual reading of the Genesis days, the firmament signifies Scripture, described in passing as 'distinguished' by history, morality and allegory. The passage prays to progress in life by it; the senses are named, not defined.

author: Hugo Rothomagensis
title: Dialogi (Hugo Rothomagensis)
senses_latin: historia > parabola > sensus mysticus > moralitas > allegoria
definitions: historia: History and parables, read or heard and held in memory; they nourish us | allegoria: Allegory, grasped by the understanding alone; by it we grow | moralitas: The moral sense, which perfects us and conforms us to the Lord
summary: A threefold scheme tied to the Trinity (number, measure, weight). History and parables nourish and are held in memory. Allegory makes us grow through the intellect. Morality perfects us. The first two are useless unless they form morals, which is Scripture's end.

author: Gerhohus Reicherspergensis
title: Commentarius aureus in Psalmos et cantica ferialia continuatio (Gerhohus Reicherspergensis)
senses_latin: historia > parabolice > littera > sensus mysticus > tropologice
example_figure: mare Rubrum; aquae quasi in utrem
summary: On Ps 77:13 (crossing of the Red Sea), Gerhoh passes over the known history, the 'bark of the letter', to seek the 'marrow' of mystical sense: the sea is baptism reddened by Christ's blood; tropologically, carnal desires restrained as in a skin.

author: Gerhohus Reicherspergensis
title: Commentarius aureus in Psalmos et cantica ferialia continuatio (Gerhohus Reicherspergensis)
senses_latin: mystice > historia > sensus moralis > spiritalis > carnaliter
example_figure: aqua versa in sanguinem; plagae Aegypti
summary: Commenting on the Egyptian plagues in Psalm 77, Gerhoh reads them mystically. Water turned into wine signifies history or the moral sense converted into the spiritual; water turned to blood signifies carnal understanding of spiritual things. The other plagues become vices.

author: Isaac de Stella
title: Epistola de anima (Isaac de Stella)
example_figure: Sapientia aedificavit sibi domum, columnae septem
summary: Reads Prov 9:1 three ways: anagogically, the natural creation of the rational mind as God's dwelling; allegorically, the Church's spiritual building; historically, as foundation, the human head (six bones) supported by seven neck vertebrae.

author: Isaac de Stella
title: Sermones (Isaac de Stella)
example_figure: nuptiae (Cana): carnis et carnis, spiritus et carnis, Verbi et hominis, Dei et mentis
summary: Isaac ranks four marriages, one per sense: flesh with flesh (historical), spirit with flesh (moral), Word with humanity (allegorical), God with the mind (anagogical). At Cana, Christ's presence at the literal wedding mystically signified the higher ones. Tropology precedes allegory.

author: Isaac de Stella
title: Sermones (Isaac de Stella)
senses_latin: sensus spiritualis > sensus physicus > sensus ethicus > historia > moralis > allegoricus > anagogicus
example_figure: hydriae capientes metretas binas vel ternas (Cana, aqua in vinum)
summary: In a Cana sermon, turning water into wine figures drawing scripture to the spiritual sense. The jars' two or three measures are the pagans' physical and ethical readings, and the Christian search beyond history for moral, allegorical and sometimes anagogical meaning.

author: Aelredus Rievallensis
title: Sermones de tempore (Aelredus Rievallensis)
definitions: anagoge: the sense concerning higher, heavenly things
summary: Ezekiel's four-faced wheel signifies Scripture, whose four faces are history, morality, allegory and anagogy. Some readers see only the plain history; seeing its unlovely parts (Judah and Tamar, David and Uriah), they despise Scripture. The Palm Sunday gospel is first considered historically.

author: Wolbero S. Pantaleonis
title: Commentaria in Canticum canticorum (Wolbero S. Pantaleonis)
summary: Scripture, the King's storehouse, is divided threefold into history, allegory and morality, suited to differing capacities. The elect pass from historical to allegorical to moral knowledge, figured by the cellars and by grain, wine and oil.

author: Wolbero S. Pantaleonis
title: Commentaria in Canticum canticorum (Wolbero S. Pantaleonis)
example_figure: cellaria regis; frumentum, vinum, oleum (granum Christus)
summary: Christ, the grain, and his works, with the wine of preaching and the oil of charity, are read 'triplici modo': historically, allegorically, morally, separately or together. This threefold reading is what 'the king brought me into his cellars' means.

author: Wolbero S. Pantaleonis
title: Commentaria in Canticum canticorum (Wolbero S. Pantaleonis)
senses_latin: historia > allegoria > moralitas > littera > sensus spiritualis > allegorice > moraliter
example_figure: murenulae aureae vermiculatae argento; rotae Ezechielis
definitions: littera: Scripture 'stands' still when understood simply according to the letter | sensus spiritualis: Scripture 'moves', like Ezekiel's wheels, when expounded allegorically or morally
summary: The golden necklaces of Cant 1:10 are the two Testaments, which bend into diverse expositions: history, allegory, morality. Like Ezekiel's wheels, Scripture stands when read literally and moves and rises when read spiritually, allegorically or morally.

author: Wolbero S. Pantaleonis
title: Commentaria in Canticum canticorum (Wolbero S. Pantaleonis)
senses_latin: litteralis > allegoricus > moralis > historicus > allegoria > moralitas > historia > mystice
example_figure: dentes sicut greges tonsarum, gemelli fetus
summary: Interpreters, the Church's teeth, grind the literal solidity of Scripture. Its 'twin offspring' are the allegorical and moral senses flowing from the letter. Scripture has a threefold sense (historical, allegorical, moral; cf. Prov 22:20), and history resolves into allegory or morality.

author: Richardus S. Victoris
title: Adnotationes mysticae in Psalmos (Richardus S. Victoris)
definitions: moralis: exhortation that builds up morals; likened to working in gold | anagogicus: demonstrates the splendour of heavenly rewards; likened to shining gems | allegoricus: searching the depths of mysteries; likened to the honeycomb | historialis: setting out truth without a veil; likened to pure honey
summary: Gold, precious stone, honeycomb and honey of the Psalm signify the fourfold sense of scripture (moral, anagogic, historical, allegorical), in which all human and angelic teaching is contained, yet the inner inspiration of God surpasses them all.

author: Richardus S. Victoris
title: Adnotationes mysticae in Psalmos (Richardus S. Victoris)
senses_latin: sensus historicus > sensus moralis > allegoria > anagoge
definitions: sensus historicus: western treasury holding the silver of eloquence; there faith is taught | sensus moralis: northern treasury of countless gems of virtues; it instructs conduct | allegoria: eastern treasury of royal ornaments, the Church's sacraments; it exercises devotion, which history prefigured | anagoge: southern treasury of the gold of heavenly wisdom; contemplation of heavenly things begins
summary: Scripture's treasury has four storehouses at the cardinal points: history (west), moral sense (north), allegory (east), anagoge (south). Each holds distinct riches and serves faith, action, devotion, contemplation. History and allegory face each other and testify mutually.

author: Richardus S. Victoris
title: Adnotationes mysticae in Psalmos (Richardus S. Victoris)
definitions: historia: teaches what was done | moralitas: teaches what we ought to do | allegoria: shows how the Church's sacraments were foretold by figures of earlier events | anagoge: contemplation of God's invisible things through created things
summary: Richard maps four sense-treasuries onto compass points. Allegory and history face and confirm each other, since history prefigures what allegory asserts. One proceeds from history to morality and from allegory to anagoge. Each sense is defined by its function.

author: Richardus S. Victoris
title: Benjamin major (Richardus S. Victoris)
senses_latin: historicus > tropologicus > allegoricus > anagogicus > historia > littera > mysticus > allegoria > tropologia > moralis > anagoge
example_figure: Mensa propositionis (table of shewbread: wood, lip, double crown)
definitions: historia: sacred history, free of all falsehood and folly, like incorruptible wood | allegoria: concerns sacraments of faith, things believed rather than understood; mystical teaching of mysteries | tropologia: moral knowledge, easily grasped by anyone, naturally inscribed in the heart | anagoge: mystical, upward-leading understanding of supercelestial things; foresight of hoped-for rewards
summary: Allegorizes the table of shewbread: gilded wood is the historical sense, the golden lip tropology, the double crown allegory and anagogy. History holds first place; mystical understanding is threefold, ranked tropology, allegory, anagogy, each defined.

author: Richardus S. Victoris
title: Expositio de tabernaculo (Richardus S. Victoris)
summary: Richard defends adding to the Fathers' literal exposition. A predecessor (likely Bede) was confident of the allegory but doubtful of the letter, and the Fathers expounded much historically, allegorically and tropologically, so some literal gaps remain to be filled.

author: Adamus Scotus
title: De tripartito tabernaculo (Adamus Scotus)
senses_latin: historia > allegoricus sensus > allegorica significatio > moralitas > mystica interpretatio > allegoria > mysticus intellectus
definitions: historia: simple narration of the words; lays the foundation of the building | allegoria: opens the mysteries of the history, raising the mind's structure into a citadel of faith | moralitas: adorns the erected building with virtues as with distinct colours
summary: Letter commissioning Adam's work: depict the tabernacle by history, expound it allegorically, then turn it to morality. Gives Gregory's building image (unnamed): history the foundation, allegory the citadel of faith, moral sense the colours.

author: Adamus Scotus
title: De tripartito tabernaculo (Adamus Scotus)
senses_latin: historia > allegoria > tropologia > sensus anagogicus > sensus historialis > sensus spiritualis
definitions: historia: milk for beginners and the tender | allegoria: bread for those advancing in faith | tropologia: solid food for those labouring in good works | sensus anagogicus: wine of contemplation for those raised to heavenly things
summary: Scripture, one and unchanging, yields diverse understandings by readers' capacity: history as milk, allegory as bread, tropology as solid food, anagogy as wine of contemplation. History, though usually easier, sometimes hides what the spiritual sense reveals, as with the tabernacle.

author: Adamus Scotus
title: De tripartito tabernaculo (Adamus Scotus)
definitions: historia: what is to be marvelled at in the literal account | allegoria: what is to be revered through the belief of perfect faith | tropologia: what is to be imitated through the holiness of good conduct
summary: Dedicatory preface: at his abbot's command Adam will show how Moses' tabernacle was physically made, then its allegorical and tropological meaning. History is to be admired, allegory venerated by faith, tropology imitated in good conduct. Church and individual soul are aligned.

author: Adamus Scotus
title: De tripartito tabernaculo (Adamus Scotus)
definitions: historia: concerns Moses' material tabernacle made on Sinai, which we are to admire | allegoria: concerns Christ's tabernacle, the Church spread through the world, which we are to venerate | tropologia: concerns the Holy Spirit's tabernacle in the pure soul, which we are to imitate
summary: Preface dividing the book into three parts. The tabernacle is read as threefold: Moses' material tabernacle (history, to admire), the Church (allegory, to venerate) and the soul (tropology, to imitate). Its circuit is the twelve tribes, twelve apostles, twelve virtues.

author: Adamus Scotus
title: De tripartito tabernaculo (Adamus Scotus)
definitions: historia: plain narration of deeds, contained on the surface of the letter, understood as read | allegoria: through the literal truth gives something else to understand about faith and Church mysteries | tropologia: like allegory rests on figurative words or deeds, but builds up morals rather than faith | anagogia: treats, in veiled or open words, the eternal joys of the heavenly homeland
summary: Scripture's understanding is fourfold: history, allegory, tropology, anagogy. Each is defined and assigned its effect on the reader (imitation, knowledge of truth, love of virtue, desire for heaven). The four are mapped onto the four feet of the tabernacle table.

author: Adamus Scotus
title: De tripartito tabernaculo (Adamus Scotus)
summary: The twelve loaves on the tabernacle table were historically always there; allegorically they signify apostolic holy men, and tropologically the twelve spiritual virtues of Gal 5 that refresh the soul. The candlestick is then read figurally of Christ.

author: Adamus Scotus
title: De tripartito tabernaculo (Adamus Scotus)
example_figure: mensa deaurata quatuor pedibus (table of the tabernacle)
definitions: historia: sets before us the holiness of exemplary deeds | allegoria: sets before us right belief of faith | anagogia: sets before us the happiness of heavenly joys
summary: In a moral reading of the tabernacle, the gilded table of reading stands for meditating on Scripture. Scripture offers holy examples in its history, right faith in allegory, and heavenly joy in anagogy.

author: Adamus Scotus
title: Epistola Adami (Adamus Scotus)
example_figure: tabernaculum Moysi / tabernaculum Christi (Ecclesia) / tabernaculum Spiritus sancti (anima fidelis)
definitions: historia: the truth of the event as it actually happened (Moses' visible tabernacle) | allegoria: the credence of sincere catholic faith (Christ's tabernacle, the Church) | tropologia: the inner purity of the secret conscience (the Spirit's tabernacle, the soul)
summary: Adam describes his tripartite tabernacle book: Moses' tabernacle belongs to history (truth of the deed), Christ's tabernacle, the Church, to allegory (faith), and the Spirit's tabernacle, the faithful soul, to tropology (purity of conscience).

author: Adamus Scotus
title: Sermones (Adamus Scotus)
example_figure: Bethlehem (house of bread): fourfold bread of sacred reading
summary: In a sermon on the monk's threefold exercise (reading, action, prayer), coming to Bethlehem stands for assiduous sacred reading. Its fourfold sense (historical, allegorical, tropological, anagogical) is tasted as a fourfold bread. The senses are named, not defined.

author: Adamus Scotus
title: Sermones (Adamus Scotus)
definitions: historia: narration of the examples of the saints, moving the mind to imitate holiness | allegoria: revelation of the truth of the faith, leading to knowledge of truth | tropologia: instruction of morals, kindling love of virtue | anagogia: revelation of heavenly joys, melting the soul with desire for supernal bliss
summary: Glossing Simeon's sword (Luke 2:35) as the word of God, Adam describes four successive strokes on the soul: history (saints' examples), allegory (faith's truth), tropology (morals), anagogy (heavenly joys), each revealing distinct thoughts.

author: Petrus Comestor
title: Historia scholastica (Petrus Comestor)
definitions: historia: the foundation of the building; has three species: annals, calendar, daybook | allegoria: wall resting on foundation; one deed figures another deed | tropologia: roof atop; from what was done it suggests what we must do | tropologia: converting discourse pertaining to the morals of the soul
summary: Prologue: Scripture is God's dining hall with three parts. History is the foundation, allegory the wall and tropology the roof. Allegory draws on persons, things, numbers, places, times and deeds (Isaac, ram, Goliath), and tropology moves more than allegory.

author: Petrus Comestor
title: Historia scholastica (Petrus Comestor)
definitions: tropologia: converting discourse concerning the moral life of the soul; moves more than allegory | allegoria: sense pertaining to the Church militant | anagoge: sense pertaining to the Church triumphant and the Trinity
summary: Ranks three senses (plainer, sharper, sweeter). Lists the sources of allegory (person, thing, number, place, time, deed) with examples such as Isaac, the ram and Goliath. Defines tropology as moral; allegory concerns the Church militant, anagoge the Church triumphant.

author: Joannes Saresberiensis
title: De VII septenis (Joannes Saresberiensis)
example_figure: Pentateuchus, Decalogus, Vetus et Novum Testamentum (numerical mysteries)
summary: In a moralized treatment of the liberal arts, the virtuous use of arithmetic is grasping scriptural numbers (five books, ten commandments, two Testaments) and thereby embracing history, allegory, tropology and anagogy. The four senses are named in passing.

author: Joannes Saresberiensis
title: Polycraticus (Joannes Saresberiensis)
senses_latin: littera > allegoria > tropologia > anagoge > sensus litterae > sensus historicus
definitions: littera: the surface of the letter, fitted to a single sense, beneath which many mysteries lie | allegoria: builds up faith from the thing signified | tropologia: builds up morals in various ways | anagoge: leads the mind upward in many ways
summary: Scripture's single literal surface hides many mysteries, because in it things, not only words, signify: allegory builds faith, tropology morals, anagoge leads upward. In the liberal arts only words signify, so readers should keep to the literal sense.

author: Gilbertus Foliot
title: Expositio in Cantica canticorum (Gilbertus Foliot)
summary: Glossing Song 5:6 'ut locutus est' via Hebrews 1:1, Foliot reads 'multisque modis' as God speaking through the prophets by mixing historical, allegorical, tropological and anagogical senses, contrasted with the Son's plain speech. The senses are named, not defined.

author: Joannes Belethus
title: Rationale divinorum officiorum (Joannes Belethus)
summary: In a liturgical discussion of readings before Easter, Beleth offers a fanciful etymology: the Lamentations are called Threni because Paschasius expounded them threefold, historically, allegorically and tropologically. He then prefers the Greek etymology, threnos meaning lament.

author: Joannes Belethus
title: Rationale divinorum officiorum (Joannes Belethus)
definitions: allegoria: other-speech or inversion: saying one thing in words, meaning another | tropologia: turning of speech toward morals | anagoge: from Greek ana (upward) and agoge (leading): a leading upward
summary: Explains the name Pascha (passage) in four senses: Israel's crossing and the destroying angel; the Church passing to faith through baptism; passing from vice to virtue by confession; Christ's and our passage to immortality. Defines three terms and adds the Jerusalem example.

author: Petrus Cellensis
title: Mystica et moralis expositio Mosaici tabernaculi (Petrus Cellensis)
summary: Among many fourfold readings of the four feet of the tabernacle table, one makes each foot a sense the reader seeks: history, allegory, morality, anagoge. The senses are named in passing, not defined.

author: Petrus Cellensis
title: Sermones (Petrus Cellensis)
example_figure: pictura domus (house adorned over fourteen days)
summary: In an allegory of building a spiritual house, the eleventh day's painting is the memory of God's works, impressed on minds by Scripture read now historically, now allegorically, now morally, like three colours.

author: Petrus Cellensis
title: Sermones (Petrus Cellensis)
example_figure: fluvius de paradiso in quatuor capita divisus
summary: In a Marian sermon on meditation, the law is likened to the paradise river dividing into four heads: letter, allegory, morality, anagogy. The Virgin hovers like a dove over these streams. The senses are named, not defined.

author: Philippus de Harveng
title: Moralitates in Cantica canticorum (Philippus de Harveng)
senses_latin: historicus > allegoria > moralitas > historialis > allegoricus > spiritualis > moralis
definitions: historica intelligentia: stripping the hide: treating the historical sense and affirming it as true | allegoria: burning the flesh: allegory understood in spiritual senses is elucidated | moralitas: offering the fat: examining morals for the benefit of faithful souls and God's praise
summary: Using the Levitical sacrifice, the hide stripped is the true historical sense, the flesh burned is allegory, the fat offered is the moral sense. Having read Jacob allegorically, he now gives the moral reading of Jacob at the well.

author: Philippus de Harveng
title: Moralitates in Cantica canticorum (Philippus de Harveng)
senses_latin: historia > moralitas > allegoria > sensus spiritualis > allegorice > moraliter > allegoricus
example_figure: puteus Isaac (Abundantia) = Vetus Testamentum; aquae = sensus spirituales
summary: Closes a moral and anagogical reading of Jacob and Rachel, then opens a second 'moralitas' mixed with allegorical flowers. Isaac's well figures the Old Testament; digging it yields abundant spiritual senses. Recalls the earlier allegorical and moral treatment.

author: Philippus de Harveng
title: Moralitates in Cantica canticorum (Philippus de Harveng)
summary: Among alternative readings of 'meliora sunt ubera tua vino', the Bride's two breasts are taken as allegory and morality in scripture, and the wine as history. These spiritual senses are sweeter than the often harsh, irrational historical understanding. Later the 'killing letter' is contrasted with spiritual knowledge.

author: Philippus de Harveng
title: Moralitates in Cantica canticorum (Philippus de Harveng)
summary: Preachers, like perfumers grinding spices, release scripture's fragrance by passing from history to allegory to morality. The king's cellars of Cant. 1 are read allegorically as the divine books, into which Christ leads us spiritually and mystically.

author: Philippus de Harveng
title: Moralitates in Cantica canticorum (Philippus de Harveng)
definitions: moralitas: the moral sense, which always accompanies and clings to our human condition | historica intelligentia: historical reading refers the verse to the earthly king David | allegoria: allegory ascribes the verse to Christ | moralitas: moral sense applied to correcting our actions
summary: Declares three things in scripture (history, allegory, morality) and applies them to Psalm 1:1: historically David, allegorically Christ, morally our actions. He then questions how the verse fits David historically, given his sin with Bathsheba.

author: Philippus de Harveng
title: Moralitates in Cantica canticorum (Philippus de Harveng)
summary: Reads Psalm 1:1 'Beatus vir' threefold: historically of David (who mourned Saul), allegorically of Christ who did not sin, morally of each of us, mapping walking, standing and sitting onto sins of thought, word and deed.

author: Garnerius Lingonensis
title: Sermones (Garnerius Lingonensis)
example_figure: Pascha, agnus paschalis (caput cum pedibus et intestinis); Pascha = transitus
summary: Easter sermon: eating the paschal lamb whole means confessing Christ as true God and man. Pascha as 'transitus' (darkness to light, unbelief to faith, vice to virtue, death to life) is celebrated as historical, allegorical, tropological and anagogical Pasch.

author: Garnerius Lingonensis
title: Sermones (Garnerius Lingonensis)
example_figure: tres scyphi in modum nucis in calamis candelabri
definitions: historia: the bare text of the narrative, which contents simpler hearers | allegoria: sense by which hearers are instructed in the faith | tropologia: sense by which hearers are built up in morals
summary: The three cups on each branch of the tabernacle lampstand signify preachers' discretion. Some hearers are content with the historical text, others need allegory to be formed in faith, others tropology to be built up in morals.

author: Garnerius Lingonensis
title: Sermones (Garnerius Lingonensis)
definitions: historia: sense lying in the signification of words to things | allegoria: sense in which things signify mystical deeds done | tropologia: sense in which things signify mystical deeds to be done
summary: Theology, served by all seven liberal arts, has three senses: history (words signifying things, served by the trivium), allegory (things signifying mystical deeds done), and tropology (deeds to be done), the latter two served by the quadrivium and physics; all teach restoration.

author: Garnerius Lingonensis
title: Sermones (Garnerius Lingonensis)
senses_latin: emphatice > antonomastice > specifice > allegorice > anagogice > tropologice > moraliter
definitions: emphatice: expressively; here the tabernacle signifies Christ, God and man | tropologice: morally; refers to the whole human being, inner and outer
summary: The tabernacle is called equivocal. It is read in six modes. Emphatically it is Christ (body, soul, divinity) and specifically the Virgin Mary. Allegorically it is the Church on earth, in purgatory and in heaven, and anagogically the angelic hierarchies. Tropologically it is the whole man.

author: Petrus Cantor
title: Verbum abbreviatum (Petrus Cantor)
summary: In a chain of sayings against superfluous glossing, Peter the Chanter recalls that Jerome expounded the whole Bible within one year historically, allegorically, tropologically and anagogically for Paula and Eustochium. The senses are named in passing.

author: Petrus Cantor
title: Verbum abbreviatum (Petrus Cantor)
summary: Galopin's editorial note says Peter the Chanter takes Rom 9's 'verbum abbreviatum' literally, then moves it to a mystical tropological or moral sense: the cutting back of excesses and vices and the bringing in of virtues. Augustine is cited in support.

author: Petrus Cantor
title: Verbum abbreviatum (Petrus Cantor)
senses_latin: historice > allegorice > littera > allegoria > moralis > anagogia
definitions: littera: teaches what was done, the events | allegoria: teaches what one should believe | moralis: teaches what one should do | anagogia: teaches where one should strive, the final goal
summary: An editorial note on Peter the Chanter's 'historice, allegorice' quotes the unattributed four-sense distich 'Littera gesta docet...' and refers the reader to Augustine's De utilitate credendi, ch. 3, for more.

author: Thomas Cisterciensis
title: Commentaria in Cantica canticorum (Thomas Cisterciensis; Joannes Algrinus)
senses_latin: sensus historicus > sensus moralis > allegoria > anagoge > historia > moralitas
definitions: historia: teaches what was done; silver of eloquence; instructs faith | moralitas: teaches what is to be done; gems of virtues; instructs action | allegoria: shows how Church sacraments were foretold by figures of earlier events | anagoge: contemplating God's invisible things through created things; gold of heavenly wisdom
summary: Scripture's treasury is divided into four storehouses at the four compass points: history (west, faith), moral sense (north, action), allegory (east, Church sacraments, devotion), anagoge (south, contemplation). Each sense is defined; the four winds of Ezekiel revive the dead.

author: Thomas Cisterciensis
title: Commentaria in Cantica canticorum (Thomas Cisterciensis; Joannes Algrinus)
definitions: moralitas: teaches how we ought to live | allegoria: makes known what was done on our behalf | anagoge: contemplates the heavenly things awaited as reward
summary: Reading the 'fullest streams' of Cant 5:12 as Scripture, the commentator grades its senses: full in morality (how to live), fuller in allegory (what was done for us), fullest in anagoge (heavenly rewards awaited).

author: Martinus Legionensis
title: Sermones de diversis (Martinus Legionensis)
summary: In an allegory of Solomon's fleet as the Church, the gold talents brought from Ophir are read as the precious sense of scripture: history, allegory, tropology and anagogy in both Testaments. The senses are named, not defined.

author: Alanus de Insulis
title: De VI alis cherubim (Alanus de Insulis)
definitions: historia: the letter as a veil covering the mystical meanings | allegoria: learning scripture's mysteries, the mind penetrates by illumination to knowledge of the divinity
summary: Reading the seraph as sacred scripture, its three pairs of wings are scripture's three senses: history, allegory, tropology. Each sense is paired because it kindles love of God and neighbour. History veils mystical meanings; allegory rises to knowledge of God.

author: Alanus de Insulis
title: Distinctiones dictionum theologicalium (Alanus de Insulis)
definitions: tropologia: the flat roof set on top, completing and perfecting the building | historia: the foundation of the building | allegoria: raises the walls upon the foundation
summary: Under the entry 'doma' (flat roof), Alanus says the word signifies tropology or morality. He cites the Historia scholastica's building image: history is the foundation, allegory raises the walls, and tropology is the roof that completes the structure.

author: Alanus de Insulis
title: Distinctiones dictionum theologicalium (Alanus de Insulis)
senses_latin: spiritualis intelligentia > spiritus > littera > mysticus sensus > historia > allegoria > tropologia
summary: In a distinctio on 'mane', one meaning is the beginning of spiritual understanding, rising from letter to spirit, to the mystical sense. Scripture is a vineyard: leaves of history, flowers of allegory, fruit of tropology.

author: Alanus de Insulis
title: Distinctiones dictionum theologicalium (Alanus de Insulis)
definitions: historia: lays the foundation of the spiritual building | allegoria: builds the walls upon that foundation | tropologia: completes the building by putting on the roof
summary: In a dictionary entry on 'tectum', Alan cites the saying that in the spiritual building history lays the foundation, allegory raises the walls and tropology finishes the roof. This is the Gregorian building image of three senses, given in passing.

author: Alanus de Insulis
title: Elucidatio in Cantica canticorum (Alanus de Insulis)
senses_latin: spiritus > littera > historia > mysticus sensus > allegoria > tropologia > spiritualis intelligentia > sensus allegoricus > intellectus moralis > interpretatio allegorica
definitions: historia: the leaves of scripture's vine: the green outer foliage | allegoria: the fragrant flower of the vine | tropologia: the fruit that satisfies, following the flower of allegory | intellectus moralis: follows allegorical interpretation as fruit follows flower, for our formation | littera: the outer rind of the pomegranate, containing spiritual fecundity within
summary: Commenting on Song 7:12, Alan reads the vineyard as scripture: rising from letter to spirit, history is the leaves, allegory the flower, tropology the fruit. Moral sense follows allegory. The pomegranate's rind is the letter, its seeds spiritual understanding.

author: Alanus de Insulis
title: Liber sententiarum (Alanus de Insulis)
definitions: historia: concerns perishable and transitory things; considered by reason | anagoge: consideration of heavenly things; a leading upward
summary: The Magi's three gifts figure three senses tied to three soul-powers. Myrrh is history, offered by reason and concerned with transitory things. Incense is tropology or morality, offered by intellect. Gold is anagoge, contemplation of heavenly things, offered by intelligence.

author: Alanus de Insulis
title: Liber sententiarum (Alanus de Insulis)
senses_latin: historica > allegorica > tropologica > historia > allegoria > tropologia
definitions: historia: likened to whey: cheaper substance, lesser flavour and delight | allegoria: likened to cheese: nourishes the soul's understanding, feeds it more solidly | tropologia: likened to butter: richer, softening, tastes sweeter to the mind's palate
summary: Milk figures sacred Scripture. As milk has three substances (whey, cheese, butter), Scripture has a threefold understanding: history (whey, lowest delight), allegory (cheese, solid nourishment of understanding) and tropology (butter, sweetest to the mind).

author: Alanus de Insulis
title: Sermones (Alanus de Insulis)
definitions: historia: the foundation: plainest, the beginning; milk for the lesser hearers | tropologia: the wall: sweeter, carries the reader forward; honey for the middling hearers | allegoria: the roof on top of the other two: sharpest, completes and perfects; solid bread for the greater hearers
summary: The master is to mix the 'three measures of flour': a threefold exposition, historical, tropological and allegorical. These are ranked as foundation, wall and roof, and as milk, honey and solid bread for lesser, middling and greater hearers.

author: Absalon Sprinckirsbacensis
title: Sermones (Absalon Sprinckirsbacensis)
senses_latin: historia > tropologia > anagoge > allegoria > intelligentia spiritalis > littera > spiritus
summary: In a moral reading of the healed woman's forty days of purification, forty is ten (the law) times four, the fourfold observance of the law: history, tropology, anagogy, allegory. The law needs spiritual understanding, since the letter kills.

author: Absalon Sprinckirsbacensis
title: Sermones (Absalon Sprinckirsbacensis)
senses_latin: spiritalis intelligentia > littera > historia > tropologia > anagoge > allegoria
definitions: historia: instructs people outwardly through commandment; shows the way of acting well; teaches obedience | tropologia: rules the soul inwardly by forming morals; shapes the will; teaches discipline | allegoria: contemplation of heavenly things; cleanses the heart through faith | anagoge: purifies the inner man by contemplating only divine things; teaches persevering love
summary: Declares the observance of four senses (history, tropology, allegory, anagogy) necessary for purifying the soul, defining each by its function and virtue; history and tropology concern neighbour, allegory and anagogy God; figured as the cherubim's four wings and four wheels.

author: Absalon Sprinckirsbacensis
title: Sermones (Absalon Sprinckirsbacensis)
example_figure: candelabrum aureum: duo latera, tres calami
summary: In a sermon on Wisdom's seven pillars, the two sides of the golden candlestick are the two Testaments founded in Christ. From each come three branches: history, tropology and allegory, a threefold understanding. The senses are named but not defined.

author: Absalon Sprinckirsbacensis
title: Sermones (Absalon Sprinckirsbacensis)
senses_latin: allegoricus intellectus > moralis intellectus > sensus litteralis > littera > spiritus
example_figure: duo pisces (with the five barley loaves); waters as Scripture
definitions: allegoricus intellectus: feeds the reader through the mysteries of Christ and the Church, to strengthen faith | moralis intellectus: concerns the forming of morals and feeds the reader toward good works
summary: Scripture is the waters. The two fish are the allegorical and moral senses, which 'leap above the waters' and draw the reader beyond the literal sense. Allegory builds faith through Christ and the Church; the moral sense builds good works.

author: Absalon Sprinckirsbacensis
title: Sermones (Absalon Sprinckirsbacensis)
example_figure: mensa (panes propositionis); four dishes (fercula) of Scripture's table
definitions: sensus historialis: instructs toward truth | moralis: shapes the will | allegoricus: strengthens faith | anagogicus: draws upward through contemplation
summary: Scripture is the table of the rich man. Its four dishes are the four senses: historical instructs to truth, moral forms the will, allegorical strengthens faith, anagogical lifts up through contemplation. Alternative divisions of the table follow.

author: Sicardus Cremonensis
title: Mitrale sive Summa de officiis ecclesiasticis (Sicardus Cremonensis)
definitions: historia: a thing narrated in plain speech, by the first signification of words | allegoria: sacraments of the Church signified by mystical words or things; 'other speech' | tropologia: moral speech for instructing or correcting conduct; 'turned speech' | anagoge: speech leading upward to future rewards and future life
summary: Allegorizing the four feet of the tabernacle table as Scripture's fourfold exposition, Sicard defines history, allegory, tropology and anagogy with etymologies and examples in plain and figured words, then distinguishes vocal (human) from real (divine) signification.

author: Sicardus Cremonensis
title: Mitrale sive Summa de officiis ecclesiasticis (Sicardus Cremonensis)
summary: In explaining the monastic twelve lessons, the number four is said to signify the monks' stability and the chariots of Aminadab, i.e. the fourfold sense of Scripture (historical, allegorical, tropological, anagogical), on which monks especially meditate.

author: Sicardus Cremonensis
title: Mitrale sive Summa de officiis ecclesiasticis (Sicardus Cremonensis)
example_figure: tria munera magorum: aurum, thus, myrrha
summary: In explaining the Epiphany, Sicard offers alternative triads that the Magi's three gifts may signify. One option is the three senses of scripture (history, tropology, allegory). They are named in passing, not defined or applied.

author: Sicardus Cremonensis
title: Mitrale sive Summa de officiis ecclesiasticis (Sicardus Cremonensis)
example_figure: quadruplex mensa: four Easter Vigil lessons (Gen 1, Exod 14, Isa 4, Haec est haereditas)
definitions: historia: teaches the simple about their own creation (literal account) | allegoria: instructs the intelligent about the manner of restoration (types of baptism) | tropologia: teaches the advanced about moral cleansing and penance | anagoge: raises the wise to heavenly things, the eternal inheritance
summary: Four Holy Saturday lessons match four kinds of faithful (simple, intelligent, advanced, wise), taught by history, allegory, tropology and anagogy respectively; each lesson is then read under its assigned sense, a fourfold table for neophytes.

author: Sicardus Cremonensis
title: Mitrale sive Summa de officiis ecclesiasticis (Sicardus Cremonensis)
summary: Reads the word Pascha as 'transitus' under four senses: historically, the angel passing over Egypt and Israel crossing out and through the Red Sea; allegorically, the Church passing by baptism to faith; tropologically, the soul passing from vice to virtue; anagogically, Christ passing from death to life.

author: Sicardus Cremonensis
title: Mitrale sive Summa de officiis ecclesiasticis (Sicardus Cremonensis)
example_figure: four Pentecost vigil lessons (Abraham; Scripsit Moyses; septem mulieres; Audi Israel)
