summary: Sicard assigns one sense to each of the four Pentecost vigil lessons. The Abraham lesson sounds history, the law of Moses allegory (the new law), the seven women tropology (good morals), and Audi Israel anagogy (eternal rejoicing).

author: Auctor incertus (Innocentius III?)
title: Commentarium in VII psalmos poenitentiales (Auctor incertus (Innocentius III?))
summary: Commenting on 'aedificabit Dominus Sion', the author says Sion is taken three ways: historically for Jerusalem, allegorically for the Church, and tropologically for the soul, each with a proof-text. He then glosses Sion as 'speculatio'.

author: Auctor incertus (Innocentius III?)
title: Commentarium in VII psalmos poenitentiales (Auctor incertus (Innocentius III?))
definitions: anagogicus: the higher Jerusalem, in the heavenly homeland | allegoricus: the lower Jerusalem, the Church on its earthly pilgrimage | tropologicus: the inner Jerusalem, within the soul | historicus: the outer Jerusalem, the city in Palestine
summary: Commenting on the psalm verse, the author says Jerusalem is taken in four ways, by four theological senses: historical, allegorical, tropological, anagogical. These are the higher, lower, inner and outer Jerusalem, each supported by a scripture text.

author: Innocentius III
title: De quadripartita specie nuptiarum (Innocentius III)
definitions: historicus: marriage between a man and his lawful wife | allegoricus: marriage between Christ and the holy Church | tropologicus: marriage between God and the just soul | anagogicus: marriage between the Word and human nature (Incarnation)
summary: Innocent states that there are four kinds of marriage corresponding to four theological senses. Historical is man and wife, allegorical is Christ and Church, tropological is God and soul, anagogical is Word and human nature. Each is proved from scripture (Gen 2, Apoc 21, Hosea 2, Song 3).

author: Innocentius III
title: Mysteria evangelicae legis et sacramenti eucharistiae (Innocentius III)
example_figure: mappula on four poles; four-headed river of paradise; four-footed table of proposition (Exod.25)
summary: In liturgical allegory, the mappula carried on four poles over the pontiff signifies Scripture expounded about Christ in four ways: history, allegory, tropology and anagogy. These are figured by paradise's four rivers and the four-footed table of proposition.

author: Innocentius III
title: Sermones communes (Innocentius III)
summary: Sermon heading announces that Gen 2:10 will be expounded in four ways: historically, allegorically, morally, anagogically. It does so through a fourfold paradise: corporal in the east, terrestrial on the way, spiritual in the mind, celestial in the homeland.

author: Innocentius III
title: Sermones communes (Innocentius III)
summary: After distinguishing four meanings of 'paradise' (celestial, terrestrial, spiritual, corporal), Innocent says the verse can be expounded in four ways. Historically, a spring waters paradise and divides into four rivers. Allegorically, the river is gospel preaching flowing from Christ.

author: Innocentius III
title: Sermones de diversis (Innocentius III)
senses_latin: historicus > allegoricus > tropologicus > anagogicus > littera > spiritus
example_figure: rationale (logion) quadrangulum duplex of the high priest
summary: The high priest's square, doubled breastplate signifies the bishop's discernment. Its four corners stand for the fourfold understanding of scripture he must have (historical, allegorical, tropological, anagogical). Its doubling stands for the two testaments, glossed with 'the letter kills, the spirit gives life'.

author: Innocentius III
title: Sermones de sanctis (Innocentius III)
example_figure: quattuor flumina paradisi (Phison, Gion, Tigris, Euphrates)
definitions: historia: literal sense in which earthly things were promised to the ancients | allegoria: sense in which the letter is changed into spirit; says one thing, means another | anagoge: sense treating chiefly heavenly things: Trinity and angelic orders | tropologia: moral sense by which the soul is planted in morals and bears fruit in works
summary: In a sermon on Gregory the Great, Scripture is the river of paradise split into four heads, matched to history (Gion), allegory (Phison), anagogy (Tigris) and tropology (Euphrates) by etymology. Each sense is defined. Gregory watered the Church with these streams.

author: Innocentius III
title: Sermones de sanctis (Innocentius III)
definitions: historia: John's carnal birth, according to nature | allegoria: John's sacramental birth, according to figure (foreknown by God) | tropologia: John's spiritual birth, according to grace (filled with the Spirit)
summary: Gabriel's words in Luke 1:13-14 carry a threefold sense matching John's threefold birth. The carnal birth follows history and nature, the sacramental birth follows allegory and figure, and the spiritual birth follows tropology and grace. Each is then developed with proof-texts.

author: Innocentius III
title: Sermones de sanctis (Innocentius III)
summary: In a sermon on Peter and Paul, the net is read as preaching, woven from diverse threads. The preacher should vary his discourse, speaking according to history, allegory, anagogy and tropology among other modes. The senses are named, not defined.

author: Innocentius III
title: Sermones de tempore (Innocentius III)
definitions: historicus: Jerusalem as the outer, earthly city in Syria | allegoricus: Jerusalem as the Church militant on its earthly way | tropologicus: Jerusalem as the faithful soul within | anagogicus: Jerusalem as the Church triumphant in the heavenly homeland
summary: Innocent says Jerusalem is taken in four ways according to four theological understandings: historical, allegorical, tropological and anagogical. These are the outer city in Syria, the Church militant, the faithful soul and the Church triumphant, each proved by scripture.

author: Innocentius III
title: Sermones de tempore (Innocentius III)
summary: Jerusalem is taken in four ways after the four theological senses. It is superior (in the homeland), inferior (on the way, the Church), interior (in the soul) and exterior (in Palestine), each with a proof text. The sermon then asks which Jerusalem 'Laetare' addresses.

author: Gregorius I
title: Commentarii in librum I Regum (Gregorius I)
summary: Closing a typical reading of Anna's canticle, in which the exalted horn is Christ's kingdom, the Church raised to angelic glory, Gregory announces a moral exposition next. Book II recalls the moral reading of the sacred history: Anna's fruitfulness as contemplation.

author: Gregorius I
title: Commentarii in librum I Regum (Gregorius I)
example_figure: Samuel minister Domino ante faciem Heli
summary: Having finished a typical (allegorical) reading of the sacred history, the converted Jews seeking the 'morsel of bread', Gregory turns to a moral reading of the same words: Samuel ministering before Eli signifies humble submission to a teacher's judgment.

author: Gregorius I
title: Homiliae in Ezechielem (Gregorius I)
senses_latin: typus > historia > moralitas > allegoria > sensus historicus > moraliter > moralis intelligentia
example_figure: turtur cuius caput retorquetur ad pennulas
summary: Gregory says the wheels rise as the reader's understanding rises: different readers seek history, morality or allegory. He reads the bush typologically of Christ, then the turtle-dove law literally (plain) and morally (mind turned to virtues, restrained from carnal pleasure).

author: Gregorius I
title: Moralia (Gregorius I)
summary: In the dedicatory letter to Leander, Gregory recalls that the brothers asked him to expound Job by drawing allegorical senses out of the words of the history, and then turning those allegories toward moral exercise.

author: Gregorius I
title: Moralia (Gregorius I)
definitions: historia: the foundation laid first | significatio typica: raises the mind's structure into the citadel of faith | moralitas: clothes the finished building as with applied colour
summary: Gregory explains his method in the Moralia. Some passages get historical exposition, some typical/allegorical, some moral, some all three. History is the foundation, typology raises the citadel of faith, morality adds colour. Some Job verses cannot be read literally.

author: Gregorius I
title: Moralia (Gregorius I)
senses_latin: historia > allegoria > sensus historicus > sensus allegoricus > sensus moralis
summary: Closing the preface, Gregory says the root of history must be fixed first so the mind may then feed on the fruit of allegories. The chapter heading announces historical, allegorical, then moral exposition, and the historical reading of Job 1:1 begins.

author: Gregorius I
title: Moralia (Gregorius I)
summary: Book heading announcing that Book III explains Job chapter 2 historically, allegorically and morally like the previous books; the first chapter, headed 'historical sense', then begins the literal narrative of Satan's second assault on Job.

author: Gregorius I
title: Moralia (Gregorius I)
example_figure: comedere et bibere vs domus luctus (Eccl. 7.3)
summary: Book III closes noting a threefold treatment. Book IV's argumentum promises to expound Job 3 historically, mystically and morally. The preface argues that the letter sometimes contradicts itself, as Ecclesiastes 2:24 against 7:3, and so drives the reader to the true sense.

author: Gregorius I
title: Moralia (Gregorius I)
example_figure: manus hostis / manus robustorum; Job pauper, oppressus, stultus
summary: Having read Job 6:23-24 briefly by allegory (the enemy's hand as Satan, the strong as evil spirits), Gregory turns to examine the historical words morally: Job as poor, oppressed and foolish for God's sake.

author: Guerricus Igniacensis
title: Sermones per annum (Guerricus Igniacensis)
summary: In a list of triads figured by the three loaves lent to the friend, Guerric says scripture can be expounded threefold, in loaves of history, allegory and morality. 'Litteralis' here means justice under the Law, not a sense.

author: Hieronymus Stridonensis
title: Epistolae (Hieronymus Stridonensis)
example_figure: judgment of Solomon: the two women and the divided child as Synagogue and Church
summary: Jerome reads the judgment of Solomon allegorically: Synagogue would divide the child between Law and Grace, the Church yields it. He then remarks that tropology's 'shadows' follow different rules from history's 'truth'.

author: Auctor incertus (Hieronymus Stridonensis?)
title: Excerpta ex commentario in Jobum (Auctor incertus (Hieronymus Stridonensis?))
senses_latin: historice > allegorice > moraliter > littera > sensus litterae > mysterium > superficies
summary: Prologue on method. Job is read historically, allegorically and morally. Some verses cannot be literal because they would be false or contradictory. Neglecting the letter elsewhere loses truth. Scripture is a river where the simple wade and the wise swim. Closely paraphrases Gregory's preface to the Moralia.

author: Auctor incertus (Hieronymus Stridonensis?)
title: Expositio interlinearis libri Job (Auctor incertus (Hieronymus Stridonensis?))
summary: An editor describes a manuscript of the pseudo-Jerome Job commentary. Its first title says some things are said historically, allegorically and morally, and the commentary is laid out in three columns. The senses are named, not defined.

author: Hieronymus Stridonensis
title: Contra Joannem Hierosolymitanum (Hieronymus Stridonensis)
summary: Jerome lists Epiphanius's charges against Origen. The sixth is that Origen so allegorizes paradise, reading angels for trees and heavenly powers for rivers, that he removes the truth of the history. No scheme of senses is stated or applied.

author: Hieronymus Stridonensis
title: Commentaria in Isaiam (Hieronymus Stridonensis)
summary: Preface to Book VIII. Jerome says books six and seven gave the allegory of the fifth volume, which he had earlier explained historically. Book VIII returns to discussing history and tropology together, according to both editions (Hebrew and Septuagint).

author: Hieronymus Stridonensis
title: Commentaria in Abacuc (Hieronymus Stridonensis)
summary: Jerome expects the charge that his historical exposition of Habakkuk 3:16 slipped into allegory and tropology. He replies that history itself is often told metaphorically, one person standing for a people, then reads the verse as the captive people's voice before turning to the LXX tropologically.

author: Hieronymus Stridonensis
title: Commentaria in Zachariam (Hieronymus Stridonensis)
summary: Preface: Origen, Hippolytus and Didymus read Zechariah wholly allegorically and scarcely touched history. Jerome instead mixes Hebrew history with Christian tropology (spiritual reading), like the householder bringing out new and old, building on rock.

author: Auctor incertus (Hieronymus Stridonensis?)
title: Breviarium in Psalmos (Auctor incertus (Augustinus Hipponensis?); Auctor incertus (Hieronymus Stridonensis?))
summary: On Psalm 75:3, the Hebrew 'umbraculum in Salem' is read tropologically: God dwells only where there is peace. Literally Sion is Jerusalem, site of the temple; tropologically and anagogically, Sion ('specula') is the soul, Church or Scripture where God dwells.

author: Auctor incertus (Hieronymus Stridonensis?)
title: Breviarium in Psalmos (Auctor incertus (Augustinus Hipponensis?); Auctor incertus (Hieronymus Stridonensis?))
example_figure: septuaginta et octoginta anni (septem et octo: Vetus et Novum Testamentum)
summary: After a literal reading of Ps 89:10 on the brevity of life, the preacher turns 'secundum anagogen.' He says every psalm admits tropology but offers a taste of spiritual meaning: seventy and eighty, seven and eight decades, signify the Old and New Testaments.

author: Joannes Cassianus
title: Collationes (Joannes Cassianus)
senses_latin: historia > intelligentia spiritalis > tropologia > allegoria > anagoge
definitions: historia: knowledge of past and visible things | allegoria: things truly done prefigured the form of another mystery | anagoge: ascends from spiritual mysteries to higher, holier secrets of heaven | tropologia: moral explanation for amending life and practical instruction
summary: Theoretical knowledge divides into historical interpretation and spiritual understanding; the spiritual has three kinds (tropology, allegory, anagogy), each defined via Galatians 4. Jerusalem is read fourfold: Jewish city, Church, heavenly city, human soul.

author: Joannes Cassianus
title: Collationes (Joannes Cassianus)
senses_latin: tropologia > historia > allegoria > anagoge > revelatio > sensus spiritualis > scientia
definitions: tropologia: moral explanation aimed at amending life and practical instruction | revelatio: belongs to allegory; unlocks by spiritual sense what the historical narrative conceals | scientia: is tropology; prudent discernment of practical matters, whether useful or honourable
summary: Defines tropology and shows the four senses converging on Jerusalem: historically the Jewish city, allegorically the Church, anagogically the heavenly city, tropologically the soul. It then maps revelation and knowledge in 1 Cor 14:6 onto allegory and tropology.

author: Eucherius Lugdunensis
title: Formulae spiritalis intelligentiae (Eucherius Lugdunensis)
senses_latin: littera > historia > sensus moralis > tropicus > intellectus superior > anagoge > tropologia
definitions: littera sive historia: the body of Scripture | sensus moralis: the soul of Scripture, also called the tropical sense | anagoge: the spirit of Scripture, the higher understanding
summary: Eucherius justifies figural reading of bodily terms for God, then sets out a threefold rule: letter/history as Scripture's body, moral (tropical) sense as soul, anagoge as spirit. He links it to the Trinity, the human person (1 Thess 5), and philosophy's three parts.

author: Eucherius Lugdunensis
title: Formulae spiritalis intelligentiae (Eucherius Lugdunensis)
senses_latin: anagoge > historia > tropologia > allegoria > spiritalis intelligentia
definitions: historia: impresses on us the truth of deeds and the reliability of the narrative | tropologia: applies mystical understandings to the amendment of life | anagoge: leads to the holier secrets of heavenly figures | allegoria: narration of deeds that foreshadowed things to come
summary: Sets out a threefold rule of scripture (history, tropology, anagoge), likened to the Trinity, to spirit/soul/body and to philosophy's physics/ethics/logic. Defines each; notes some add allegory as a fourth. Illustrates with heaven and waters, then divides contemplative knowledge into historical and spiritual.

author: Eucherius Lugdunensis
title: Instructiones (Eucherius Lugdunensis)
definitions: anagoge: the higher sense | tropologia: moral understanding
summary: Within a glossary of Greek ecclesiastical terms, Eucherius glosses anagoge as the higher sense and tropologia as moral understanding. 'Historiae' under Paralipomenon means narratives, not a sense. No scheme of senses is stated.

author: Facundus Hermianensis
title: Pro defensione trium capitulorum (Facundus Hermianensis)
summary: Facundus defends Theodore of Mopsuestia, accused of expounding Psalms morally rather than christologically; he notes that moral exposition of prophecies is often praised, and cites Theodore's own retraction from his book De allegoria et historia against Origen.

author: Auctor incertus (Cassiodorus Vivariensis?)
title: Expositio in Cantica canticorum (Auctor incertus (Cassiodorus Vivariensis?))
senses_latin: spiritualis intelligentia > littera > allegoria > moralitas > anagoge
definitions: anagoge: the higher sense | spiritualis intelligentia: spiritual understanding contained within the letter, like honey in wax
summary: Glossing the dripping honeycomb (Song 4:11), the commentator likens the spiritual sense in the letter to honey in wax. Scripture 'drips' because it is understood in many ways: by letter, allegory, morality, and anagoge (the higher sense).

author: Auctores varii
title: Testimonia (Auctores varii)
summary: Sigebert of Gembloux's catalogue entry on Gregory the Great reports that, at Leander's request, Gregory expounded Job threefold: historically, allegorically and morally (the Moralia). The senses are named in passing, not defined or applied.

author: Gregorius I
title: Homiliae in Evangelia (Gregorius I)
definitions: historia: the truth of the narrative, the root that grounds allegory; it builds up morals | allegoria: spiritual understanding, sought after the history, which builds up faith | moralitas: moral teaching drawn from the history, needed by the hearers
summary: Gregory says history's truth comes first and roots allegory's fruit. Allegory builds faith, history builds morals. He reverses the order for believers: allegory first (Dives as the Jews, Lazarus as the Gentiles), morality last.

author: Isidorus Hispalensis
title: De fide Catholica (Isidorus Hispalensis)
senses_latin: historialiter > mysticus sensus > spiritualiter > historia > sacramentorum intelligentia > mystice > moraliter > informatio morum
definitions: mysticus sensus: the mystical sense is the spiritual understanding | moraliter: teaches what one ought to do in each matter | sacramentorum intelligentia: understanding of the sacraments (mysteries), following the historical sense
summary: Argues that the law must be read not only historically but mystically. Using Proverbs' 'write it twofold and threefold', it posits history and mystery, then adds morals. Noah's two- and three-chambered ark figures the same scheme.

author: Isidorus Hispalensis
title: Sententiae (Isidorus Hispalensis)
senses_latin: historia > tropologia > mystice > littera > moraliter > spiritaliter
definitions: historice: according to the letter | tropologice: according to moral knowledge | mystice: according to spiritual understanding
summary: Isidore states that the divine law is to be understood in a threefold way: historically (by the letter), tropologically (moral knowledge), mystically (spiritual understanding). Faith is held historically yet must also be interpreted morally and understood spiritually.

author: Aldhelmus Schireburnensis
title: De laudibus virginitatis (Aldhelmus Schireburnensis)
senses_latin: mysticus > spiritualiter > historia > allegoria > tropologia > anagoge
summary: In praising the nuns' studies, Aldhelm says they examine the Gospels as expounded mystically and spiritually by the catholic Fathers, arranged by the fourfold rule of church tradition: history, allegory, tropology, anagoge. The senses are named, not defined.

author: Beda
title: De schematibus et tropis sacrae Scripturae (Beda)
senses_latin: mystice > historia > typicus > tropologia > moralis > anagoge > sensus spiritualis > sensus mysticus > allegoria
definitions: tropologia: the moral sense, a moral rule or perfection | anagoge: the sense that leads upward to higher, heavenly things | allegoria: strictly, figurative sayings or deeds concerning Christ or the Church (Gregory's usage)
summary: Treating allegory as a trope, Bede says allegory of deed or word can signify a historical, typical, tropological or anagogical meaning. He illustrates each, then reads the temple and Jerusalem under all four senses, following Gregory's restriction of 'allegoria' to Christ and the Church.

author: Beda
title: Allegorica expositio in Cantica canticorum (Beda)
senses_latin: sensus spiritualis > littera > intelligentia spiritualis > allegoria > tropologia > sensus moralis > anagoge
definitions: sensus spiritualis: the honey hidden within the wax of the letter | tropologia: the moral sense | anagoge: understanding that leads upward to higher things
summary: Glossing the honeycomb of Cant 4:11 as spiritual sense within the letter, Bede illustrates scripture's fecundity with Jerusalem read by letter (city), allegory (Church), tropology (holy soul), anagogy (heavenly homeland), noting graded fitness.

author: Beda
title: Allegorica expositio in Samuelem (Beda)
definitions: historia: the first, historical reading, fulfilled through the Law before Christ's incarnation | allegoricus: sense fitting the truth of present grace | anagogicus: sense fitting the beatitude of the future life | littera: things said or done openly, without any veil
summary: Bede reads the three loaves of 1 Sam 10 as threefold Scripture. The two loaves given to Saul are the twofold allegorical and anagogical sense opened by Christ after the historical reading. He links this to Luke 11's three loaves and Leviticus 2's three cookings, the gridiron being the letter.

author: Beda
title: Commentarii in Pentateuchum (Beda)
summary: Reads the Passover lamb precepts of Exodus 12 phrase by phrase, alternating historical (month of Christ's passion), mystical (Christ, Church, sacraments) and moral readings (observing Christ in the heart, ignorance of sin, compunction).

author: Beda
title: De tabernaculo et vestibus sacerdotum (Beda)
senses_latin: historicus > allegoricus > tropologicus > moralis > anagogicus > historia > allegoria > tropologia
definitions: historia: plain narration of how something was literally done or said | allegoria: words or mystic things signifying the sacraments of Christ and the Church | tropologia: moral speech, plain or figurative, aimed at forming and correcting conduct
summary: The tabernacle table's four feet signify the fourfold sense of scripture: historical, allegorical, tropological (moral), anagogical. Bede defines history, allegory (in words, Isa 11:1, and in things, the Exodus) and tropology (plain, 1 John 3:18; figurative, Eccl 9:8).

author: Beda
title: Hexaemeron (Beda)
senses_latin: historicus > allegoricus > anagogicus > historia > allegoria > anagoge
example_figure: decor domus Dei (Solomon's temple, the Church, the heavenly home); tria sata similae
definitions: anagoge: the sense that leads the mind upward to heavenly things
summary: Reading Sara's three measures of flour (Gen 18:6), Bede states that scripture has a threefold sense (historical, allegorical, anagogical). He illustrates it with 'the beauty of thy house': Solomon's temple, the Church, and the heavenly home. All three senses aim at charity.

author: Beda
title: In Evangelium S. Matthaei (Beda)
senses_latin: mystice > sensus spiritalis > allegoria > historia > anagoge
summary: Commenting on the Magi's gifts, Beda gives several readings. Among them he reports that unnamed others take the gifts as signs of three senses: gold for allegory, myrrh for history, frankincense for anagogy. He defines none of them.

author: Heterius Uxamensis
title: Epistola (Heterius Uxamensis; Beatus)
senses_latin: littera > historia > tropologia > mystica intelligentia > sensus moralis > tropicus > anagoge > allegoria
example_figure: Ambulabat Dominus; Descendit Dominus; Juravit Dominus per animam suam
definitions: littera: the body of scripture; the history read and heard, outward sense | tropologia: the soul of scripture, the moral sense | mystica intelligentia: the spirit of scripture, higher angelic understanding called anagoge
summary: Paralleling man as body, soul and spirit (after the Apostle), scripture has three parts: letter/history (body), tropology/moral sense (soul), mystical understanding/anagoge (spirit). Reading only literally is carnal, yet some history must stand and not be allegorized.

author: Heterius Uxamensis
title: Epistola (Heterius Uxamensis; Beatus)
senses_latin: historia > moralis scientia > spiritus > tropologia > mystica intelligentia > spiritualis intelligentia
definitions: historia: the body of the letter, like the human body | moralis scientia: moral sense, in the history as the soul is in the body | spiritus: spiritual sense, within the moral sense, where God is found
summary: Contemplative life ascends from history (body of the letter) to moral sense (soul) to spirit, where God is found. The whole book, like the whole man and the whole Christ, needs all three; remove one and Christ is lost.

author: Julianus Toletanus
title: Commentarius in Nahum (Julianus Toletanus)
summary: Preface to Nahum giving a fourfold reading of the book. Historically it treats the destruction of Nineveh; allegorically, the desolation of the world; mystically, humanity's restoration through Christ; morally, the fallen sinner's restoration to former or greater dignity.

author: Julianus Toletanus
title: Commentarius in Nahum (Julianus Toletanus)
example_figure: Onus Ninive, liber visionis Nahum Elchesei
summary: Reads Nahum's title historically (Nineveh's fall to the Chaldeans, restoration under Ezra and Nehemiah), then mystically or morally: world's conflagration, resurrection and glorification; damnation, election and praise; unbelief, conversion, consummation.

author: Julianus Toletanus
title: Commentarius in Nahum (Julianus Toletanus)
summary: Nineveh can be taken four ways: historically as the famed Assyrian capital, allegorically as the world, mystically as a type of the Church, and morally as the soul. The historical sense was already treated; the others follow.

author: Carolus Magnus
title: De imaginibus (Carolus Magnus)
summary: Against the iconophiles, the house of God in 'Domine, dilexi decorem domus tuae' is read allegorically as the Church, anagogically as the heavenly homeland, and tropologically as the human soul. It is a spiritual dwelling, not material walls or images.

author: Carolus Magnus
title: De imaginibus (Carolus Magnus)
summary: Against image-worship, the Libri Carolini say many scriptural texts could show the Church's beauty according to tropology, allegory and anagogy, but brevity forbids. The beauty of God's house lies in spiritual virtues, not material images.

author: Alcuinus
title: Interpretationes nominum Hebraicorum (Alcuinus)
senses_latin: allegoricus sensus > moralis sensus > interpretatio litteralis
summary: Introducing Hebrew name interpretations for Christ's genealogy, the homily says the names hold allegorical and moral meanings. A 'literal interpretation' heading then gives the bare etymologies. The senses are named, not defined or applied.

author: Alcuinus
title: Confessio fidei (Alcuinus)
senses_latin: historia > sensus spiritualis > historialis > allegoricus > moralis sensus
definitions: historialis modus: mode that only reports things that happened | allegoricus: mode where the historical order cannot stand literally | ex utrisque compositus: mixed mode, valid both historically and allegorically | moralis sensus: moral sense drawn from scripture, best teaching, amends life and conduct
summary: Within a profession of faith, the author affirms the historical truth of scripture while seeking its spiritual sense. Scripture is historical, allegorical, or both, and a moral sense is sometimes drawn from it for amending life.

author: Sedulius Scotus
title: Collectanea in omnes B. Pauli epistolas (Sedulius Scotus)
senses_latin: revelatio > allegoricus > scientia > tropologicus > moralis > prophetia > anagogicus > doctrina > historia > littera
definitions: allegoricus sensus: revelation: something about the future revealed under a figure, e.g. the cloud as baptism | tropologicus vel moralis sensus: Paul's 'knowledge': moral teaching, e.g. praying with head veiled | anagogicus sensus: Paul's 'prophecy': foretelling last things, e.g. the future resurrection of bodies | historia secundum litteram: Paul's 'doctrine': plain historical teaching, e.g. Christ lived, died, rose
summary: Glossing 1 Cor 14:6, Sedulius maps Paul's revelation, knowledge, prophecy and doctrine onto the allegorical, tropological, anagogical and literal-historical senses. Each is illustrated from Paul: the cloud as baptism, the veiled head, those who sleep, and Christ's death and resurrection.

author: Sedulius Scotus
title: Collectanea in omnes B. Pauli epistolas (Sedulius Scotus)
summary: Commenting on Galatians 4, Sedulius says the single name Jerusalem signifies four figures: historically the Jewish city, allegorically Christ's Church, anagogically the heavenly city of God, and tropologically the human soul.

author: Theutmirus
title: Quaestiones super libros Regum (Theutmirus; Claudius Taurinensis)
summary: A letter by Theutmirus asks Claudius to explain his questions on Kings according to history, allegory and tropology: first what holds historically, second what allegory admits, third the moral sense throughout. Bede's thirty questions are mentioned.

author: Symphosius Amalarius
title: De ecclesiasticis officiis (Symphosius Amalarius)
senses_latin: historicus > allegoricus > tropologicus > moralis > anagogicus > historia > littera
definitions: historia: plain narration of how something was done or said according to the letter
summary: Amalarius quotes Bede's De tabernaculo: the four feet of the tabernacle table signify the fourfold sense (historical, allegorical, tropological or moral, anagogical). He defines history and maps the four Holy Saturday lessons onto the feet, beginning with Genesis as history.

author: Symphosius Amalarius
title: De ecclesiasticis officiis (Symphosius Amalarius)
definitions: tropologia: speech that treats of morals, of conduct
summary: In the night office, the psalms are a tropological (moral) utterance. The lessons that follow contain history, allegory, tropology and anagoge. The psalms' tropology recalls our own works, the lessons' tropology the works of others.

author: Rabanus Maurus
title: Commentarium in Matthaeum (Rabanus Maurus)
summary: In an allegorical reading of the Magi, the three gifts drawn from their treasures are said to signify physics, ethics and logic, or history, tropology and allegory, or faith in the Trinity. The senses are named, not defined.

author: Rabanus Maurus
title: Commentaria in Exodum (Rabanus Maurus)
definitions: historia: plain narration of how something was literally done or said | allegoria: mystical words or things signify the sacraments of Christ and the Church | tropologica: moral speech, open or figurative, aimed at instructing and correcting conduct
summary: The table's four feet signify the fourfold way scripture is taken: historical, allegorical, tropological (moral), anagogical. History, allegory (by words, Isa 11, or things, the Exodus) and tropology are defined with examples. Text silently follows Bede's De tabernaculo.

author: Rabanus Maurus
title: Enarratio super Deuteronomium (Rabanus Maurus)
senses_latin: littera > sensus spiritalis > historialiter > moraliter > allegoria
example_figure: seges amici (spicas frangere, falce non metere)
definitions: historialiter: passages that, read historically, instill faith | moraliter: passages that train the reader for holy living | allegoria: passages that, read not by history but allegorically, reveal venerable mysteries
summary: Plucking ears in a friend's field means bringing the letter of the law to its spiritual sense where fitting; reaping with a sickle means twisting all scripture. Some passages teach faith historically, some morals, some allegorical mysteries. Discernment is needed.

author: Rabanus Maurus
title: Enarratio super Deuteronomium (Rabanus Maurus)
example_figure: maledictiones (advena, pupillus, vidua; uxor patris; jumentum; soror; socrus)
summary: Reads the curses of Deuteronomy 27 in turn. Literally, unjust judgment and incest are forbidden. Allegorically the stranger, orphan and widow are spiritual figures, and the father's wife is Christ's bride corrupted by heretics. Tropologically, do not imitate a father's misdeeds.

author: Rabanus Maurus
title: Enarratio super Deuteronomium (Rabanus Maurus)
senses_latin: historia > spiritalis intelligentia > allegoria > tropologia > theoria
definitions: historia: literal account preserving scripture's truth; here Moses reproaching Israel's faithlessness despite God's benefits | allegoria: teaching the Church about heavenly mysteries | tropologia: moral exhortation of each believer to upright conduct; learning useful good disciplines | theoria: heavenly contemplation, insight into hidden divine things, reached through the threefold distinction
summary: The Song of Moses is not mere history but full of spiritual meaning. Its history, allegory and tropology each have a role, and this threefold distinction lifts the sober reader to heavenly theoria, divine contemplation.

author: Rabanus Maurus
title: Commentaria in Ecclesiasticum (Rabanus Maurus)
senses_latin: mysticus > spiritalis intelligentia > historia > moralitas > allegoria
definitions: historia: the historical sense of this book teaches morals | allegoria: the allegorical sense instructs in the sacrament of faith
summary: Commenting on Sirach 24:46, Rabanus says the verse shows the book is mystical and needs spiritual understanding. Its history teaches morals and its allegory instructs in the sacrament of faith, so it is useful to all readers.

author: Rabanus Maurus
title: Commentaria in Ecclesiasticum (Rabanus Maurus)
senses_latin: mysticus sensus > allegoria > historica narratio > moralitas > anagoge > spiritaliter
summary: Glossing Sirach 39 on the sage who explores hidden parables, Rabanus says the churchman seeks the mystical sense, uncovering allegory hidden in the historical narrative and discerning its moral use and its allegorical and anagogical spiritual meaning.

author: Rabanus Maurus
title: Commentaria in Ecclesiasticum (Rabanus Maurus)
summary: Transitional remark: the author (Sirach) has so far treated much morally and touched on allegory and anagogy in setting out divine mysteries. Now he turns to praising the fathers (Sir. 44). The senses are named in passing.

author: Rabanus Maurus
title: Commentaria in Paralipomena (Rabanus Maurus)
senses_latin: spiritualiter > littera > figuraliter > historia > allegoria > tropologia > anagoge
summary: The cithara figures the Church, whose preachers sound Old and New Testament now by the letter, now figuratively. The lyre's varied notes are the Church's teaching through history, allegory, tropology and anagogy, which stay in harmony.

author: Rabanus Maurus
title: Commentaria in Paralipomena (Rabanus Maurus)
example_figure: classis Salomonis in Ophir; quadringenta quinquaginta talenta auri
summary: Solomon's fleet is read as the Church. Bringing gold from Ophir signifies seeking precious meaning beneath the cheap letter. The 450 talents are the precious sense of history, allegory, tropology and anagoge, found through the Spirit's grace.

author: Rabanus Maurus
title: Commentaria in libros Regum (Rabanus Maurus)
example_figure: Classis Salomonis in Ophir; quadringenta viginti talenta auri
summary: Allegorizing Solomon's fleet as the Church, Rabanus reads the gold fetched from Ophir as the precious sense sought beneath the lowly letter. He names history, allegory, tropology and anagoge, found in both testaments, without defining them.

author: Rabanus Maurus
title: Commentaria in librum Sapientiae (Rabanus Maurus)
definitions: anagoge: what it intimates about heavenly, supernal things
summary: Commenting on Wisdom 7 and Solomon's wisdom, Rabanus says Christ, the true Solomon, gives his disciples full understanding of what history teaches, allegory shows, tropology commends and anagogy intimates about heavenly things. The four senses are named in passing, not expounded.

author: Rabanus Maurus
title: De universo (Rabanus Maurus)
senses_latin: mystice > typus > historia > allegorice > tropologice > anagoge
summary: Reads Jerusalem in four senses. Historically it is the city where Christ died and rose. Allegorically it is the present Church, tropologically the faithful soul contemplating God, and anagogically the heavenly homeland. Judaea is also read mystically as the Church.

author: Rabanus Maurus
title: De universo (Rabanus Maurus)
senses_latin: historia > allegoria > tropologia > anagoge > sensus mysticus
summary: Jerusalem has four significations in Scripture: historically the earthly city, allegorically the Church, tropologically the faithful soul, anagogically the heavenly homeland. Sion likewise bears a mystical sense: historically the Jewish people or city, allegorically the Church, anagogically the heavenly homeland.

author: Auctor incertus (Rabanus Maurus?)
title: Allegoriae in universam sacram scripturam (Auctor incertus (Rabanus Maurus?))
senses_latin: historia > allegoria > tropologia > anagogia > moralitas > littera
example_figure: quatuor filiae matris Sapientiae; domus animae (fundamentum, parietes, tectum, ornatus)
definitions: historia: fitting narration of things done, contained in the surface of the letter, understood as read | allegoria: saying one thing, signifying another: the faith and mysteries of the Church, present or future | tropologia: figurative sayings or deeds that build up morals, as allegory builds up faith | anagogia: concerns eternal joys of the heavenly homeland, in veiled or open words
summary: Prologue setting out four senses as four daughters of Mother Wisdom: milk of history, bread of allegory, tropology's refreshment, anagogy's wine. Each is defined, its effect stated, and a house image given. Texts may bear one to four senses.

author: Auctor incertus (Rabanus Maurus?)
title: Allegoriae in universam sacram scripturam (Auctor incertus (Rabanus Maurus?))
senses_latin: metonymia > allegoria > tropologia > sensus moralis > anagoge
definitions: tropologia: the moral sense | anagoge: understanding that leads toward higher, heavenly things
summary: Within a dictionary entry, Jerusalem is read fourfold: by metonymy its inhabitants, allegorically the Church, tropologically the holy soul, anagogically the heavenly homeland. The last three share the meaning 'vision of peace', though earthly and heavenly peace differ.

author: Auctor incertus (Rabanus Maurus?)
title: Allegoriae in universam sacram scripturam (Auctor incertus (Rabanus Maurus?))
summary: A dictionary entry glosses the widow's quadrans (two mites) as the fourfold understanding of scripture: the Church honours two Testaments, in which understanding is fourfold, historical, allegorical, tropological, anagogical. The senses are named, not defined.

author: Rabanus Maurus
title: Allegoriae in universam sacram scripturam (Rabanus Maurus)
example_figure: quatuor filiae matris Sapientiae; lac, panis, refectio, vinum; domus animae (fundamentum, parietes, tectum, ornatus)
definitions: historia: apt narration of deeds done, on the surface of the letter, understood as read | allegoria: saying one thing, signifying another: the mysteries of faith and the Church, present or future | tropologia: figurative like allegory but builds up morals rather than faith | anagoge: concerns the eternal joys of the heavenly homeland, in veiled or open words
summary: Preface sets out four understandings of scripture (history, allegory, tropology, anagogy) as four daughters of Mother Wisdom feeding the soul with milk, bread, food and wine. It defines each and likens them to a house: foundation, walls, roof, decoration.

author: Rabanus Maurus
title: Allegoriae in universam sacram scripturam (Rabanus Maurus)
senses_latin: metonymia > allegoria > tropologia > sensus moralis > anagoge > intelligentia ad superiora
definitions: tropologia: the moral sense | anagoge: understanding that leads upward to higher things
summary: In the dictionary entry on Jerusalem, it reads the word fourfold. By metonymy it is the city's inhabitants, allegorically the Church, tropologically the holy soul, anagogically the heavenly homeland. Each sense has its own proof-text, unified by 'visio pacis'.

author: Rabanus Maurus
title: Allegoriae in universam sacram scripturam (Rabanus Maurus)
summary: In a distinctio entry, the widow's quadrans (two mites) signifies the fourfold understanding of scripture. The Church honours both Testaments, whose understanding is fourfold: historical, allegorical, tropological and anagogical.

author: Rabanus Maurus
title: Commentaria in Cantica (Rabanus Maurus)
senses_latin: historia > intelligentia spiritualis > allegoria > tropologia > theoria
definitions: historia: literal account rebuking Israel's faithlessness; preserves the truth of Scripture | allegoria: instructs the Church about heavenly mysteries | tropologia: moral sense urging each believer to upright conduct; teaches useful disciplines | theoria: heavenly contemplation of hidden things, reached through the threefold distinction
summary: Prefacing Moses' Deuteronomy canticle, the text says it is not mere history but full of spiritual meaning: history rebukes Israel, allegory teaches the Church heavenly mysteries, tropology moves to morals; this tripartite distinction leads to heavenly contemplation.

author: Anselmus Laudunensis et schola
title: Liber Deuteronomii (Anselmus Laudunensis et schola; Glossa ordinaria)
definitions: historialiter: some scriptural places instill faith through their historical account | moraliter: some places instruct holy conduct of life | allegoria: some places, not by history but by allegory, reveal venerable mysteries
summary: Glossing entry into a neighbour's grain field, the gloss says scripture's passages differ: some build faith historically, some teach conduct morally, some show mysteries allegorically rather than historically. The reader must therefore pluck with discernment.

author: Anselmus Laudunensis et schola
title: Liber Deuteronomii (Anselmus Laudunensis et schola; Glossa ordinaria)
definitions: historia: the literal level, where Moses reproaches ungrateful Israel; its truth must be kept | allegoria: instructs the holy Church; the place of mysteries | tropologia: calls to moral uprightness; the usefulness of discipline | theoria: heavenly contemplation, the goal reached through the other three senses
summary: Moses' song is not to be taken simply. Historically it rebukes Israel, allegorically it instructs the Church, tropologically it moves to virtue. Keep truth in history, mysteries in allegory, discipline in tropology, rising to heavenly theoria. Rabanus: heavens hear allegory, earth history.

author: Anselmus Laudunensis et schola
title: Liber Ecclesiasticus (Anselmus Laudunensis et schola; Glossa ordinaria)
definitions: historice: read historically, the book teaches moral conduct | allegorice: read allegorically, it teaches the sacrament (mystery) of the faith
summary: Gloss on Ecclus 24:46, credited to Rabanus: the book is mystical and profitable to read. Taken historically it teaches morals; taken allegorically, the sacrament of faith. An earlier 'tropice' only marks figurative speech about the Father.

author: Anselmus Laudunensis et schola
title: Liber Exodus (Anselmus Laudunensis et schola; Glossa ordinaria)
senses_latin: littera > mystice > historia > moralitas > allegoria > allegorice
example_figure: funiculus triplex (funes of the tabernacle, Exod 38:20)
summary: The gloss reads the tabernacle pegs literally, then mystically. The cords are Scripture, the 'threefold cord' of Ecclesiastes, which stands on history, morality and allegory and cannot be broken by heretics. Exod 40:1 is then read literally and allegorically.

author: Anselmus Laudunensis et schola
title: Liber III Regum (Anselmus Laudunensis et schola; Glossa ordinaria)
summary: The Gloss reads Solomon's fleet as the Church. An abbreviated citation ends with history, allegory, tropology and anagogy in both Testaments, named in passing within the figurative reading. The Queen of Sheba section is headed 'Allegorice'. No scheme is defined.

author: Anselmus Laudunensis et schola
title: Liber Job (Anselmus Laudunensis et schola; Glossa ordinaria)
senses_latin: historice > allegorice > moraliter > littera > sensus litterae > allegoria
summary: Gregorian prothemata: Job is read historically, allegorically and morally. Some verses cannot be taken literally (absurd or contradictory, e.g. Job 9:13, 7:15, 3:3), yet neglecting the letter, as in seeking allegory in Job 31's works of mercy, loses truth. Scripture is a river where lamb wades and elephant swims.

author: Anselmus Laudunensis et schola
title: Liber Paralipomenon I (Anselmus Laudunensis et schola; Glossa ordinaria)
senses_latin: littera > figuraliter > historia > allegoria > tropologia > anagoge
summary: Glossing the Levites' instruments, the cithara (Church) is played 'otherwise in the letter, otherwise in the sense'. The lyre signifies the Church, whose varied teaching sounds historically, allegorically, tropologically and anagogically yet stays in harmony.

author: Nicolaus de Lira
title: Prologus de commendatione Sacrae Scripturae (Nicolaus de Lira)
senses_latin: sensus litteralis > sensus historicus > sensus mysticus > sensus spiritualis > sensus allegoricus > sensus moralis > sensus tropologicus > sensus anagogicus
definitions: sensus litteralis: the sense signified by the words themselves | sensus mysticus: the sense signified by the things the words signify; threefold | sensus allegoricus: things signify what is to be believed in the new law | sensus moralis: things signify what we must do | sensus anagogicus: things signify what is hoped for in future beatitude; from anago, to lift up
summary: Scripture alone has one letter with several senses because God makes things, not just words, signify. Literal/historical sense from words; mystical sense from things, threefold: allegorical (belief), moral (action), anagogical (hope). Cites the distich and Jerusalem example.

author: Nicolaus de Lira
title: Prologus in moralitates Bibliorum (Nicolaus de Lira)
senses_latin: sensus litteralis > sensus mysticus > allegoricus > moralis > anagogicus > parabolicus
definitions: sensus litteralis: the sense signified by the words themselves | sensus mysticus: the sense signified by the things the words signify; threefold | allegoricus: mystical sense pertaining to what is to be believed | moralis: mystical sense pertaining to what is to be done | anagogicus: mystical sense pertaining to things hoped for in future beatitude; leading upward | parabolicus: the first sense where no verbal literal sense exists; loosely called literal
summary: Scripture is written within and without: literal sense by words, mystical by things, the latter threefold (allegorical, moral, anagogical). Cites the distich; Jerusalem example; per Cassian not every passage has all four; parabolic sense loosely literal; Abraham's sons, lion.

author: Paulus de Sancta Maria
title: Additiones (Paulus de Sancta Maria)
senses_latin: sensus litteralis > sensus spiritualis > sensus allegoricus > sensus anagogicus > sensus tropologicus > historia > littera > allegoria > tropologia > anagogia
example_figure: Descendit Deus ut videret civitatem et turrim
definitions: sensus allegoricus: teaches what is to be believed, pertaining to faith | sensus anagogicus: teaches what is to be hoped for, pertaining to hope | sensus tropologicus: teaches what is to be done, pertaining to charity | sensus litteralis: conveys only history; taken from the first signification by which words signify things | sensus spiritualis: founded on things signified by the letter signifying further things
summary: Scholastic quaestio whether the literal sense is worthier than the others; objections argue spiritual senses superior, mapping allegory/anagogy/tropology to faith/hope/charity, citing the distich Littera gesta docet, the foundation-building image, and anthropomorphic falsehoods in the letter.

author: Paulus de Sancta Maria
title: Additiones (Paulus de Sancta Maria)
senses_latin: sensus spiritualis > sensus litteralis > allegoria > anagoge > historialiter > moralis > sensus historicus > sensus etymologicus > sensus anagogicus
definitions: sensus litteralis: sense taken from what the words signify | sensus spiritualis: sense taken from the things signified by the words | allegorice: referring what is said of Christ to his mystical body | moraliter: referring it to our acts, which are to be ruled by Christ | anagogice: insofar as Christ shows us the way to glory | sensus historicus: the letter expounded simply (Augustine's literal subdivision) | sensus etymologicus: giving the cause of what the letter contains | sensus anagogicus: showing the letter does not contradict another scripture's truth
summary: Argues, after Aquinas's Quodlibet, that not every passage has four senses: precepts, Christ's interpretations and Pauline epistles are literal only; graded scheme of which texts admit how many senses; then Augustine's threefold literal sense (historical, etymological, anagogical).

author: Paulus de Sancta Maria
title: Additiones (Paulus de Sancta Maria)
senses_latin: sensus litteralis > sensus mysticus > spiritus > littera > tropologicus > anagogicus > allegoricus > spiritualis intelligentia
definitions: tropologicus: the mystical sense that concerns morals | anagogicus: the mystical sense concerning faith in the Godhead | allegoricus: the mystical sense concerning faith in Christ's humanity
summary: Rebuts claims that the literal sense is worthier than the mystical on grounds of extension, universality and certainty. Spiritual sense extends further, and literal is incommunicable while mystical multiplies, per Hales: morals (tropological), Godhead (anagogical), humanity (allegorical).

author: Paulus de Sancta Maria
title: Additiones (Paulus de Sancta Maria)
senses_latin: sensus litteralis > sensus mysticus > sensus allegoricus > sensus tropologicus > sensus spiritualis > allegoria
definitions: sensus allegoricus: the sense conveying what is to be believed | sensus tropologicus: the sense conveying what is to be done
summary: Argues against an opponent that the literal sense contains all things to be believed and done, including the sacraments. Nothing necessary to faith or morals lies in the spiritual sense that is not plainly taught literally elsewhere. Christ always cited scripture literally.

author: Paulus de Sancta Maria
title: Additiones (Paulus de Sancta Maria)
senses_latin: sensus litteralis > sensus mysticus > tropologicus > allegoricus > anagogicus > historica > etymologica > anagogica > sensus spiritualis
definitions: tropologicus: treats only of things to be done in morals | allegoricus: treats of things to be believed | anagogicus: treats of things to be hoped for | sensus litteralis: treats all the above matters and also past deeds
summary: Polemic for the preeminence of the literal sense: precepts like Deut 6 have only a literal sense; mystical senses are each limited (tropology morals, allegory faith, anagogy hope), while the literal is universal and multipliable, with Augustinian species (historical, etymological, anagogical); certainty of mystical sense needs no sanctifying grace.

author: Angelomus Luxovensis
title: Enarrationes in Cantica canticorum (Angelomus Luxovensis)
senses_latin: spiritualis intellectus > historialiter > allegoria > moralis intellectus > theorica
summary: Preface to Emperor Lothar, following Gregory's 'machina' image: God speaks through enigmas to lift the torpid soul. He asks the emperor to seek nothing historical in the Song, only allegories, with moral understanding added for relief.

author: Angelomus Luxovensis
title: Enarrationes in libros Regum (Angelomus Luxovensis)
definitions: historia: sets out the deeds that were done | allegoria: allegorical signification that builds up faith | moralitas: moral sense that orders an upright life
summary: After distinguishing figurative modes (one moral only, one also referring to faith), Angelomus states his method for Kings: a threefold division of history (deeds), allegory (builds faith) and morality (honest life). A verse prologue then promises typical and mystical senses.

author: Angelomus Luxovensis
title: Enarrationes in libros Regum (Angelomus Luxovensis)
senses_latin: historia > spiritalis intelligentia > moralis > allegoria > moralitas > spiritalis intellectus
summary: Angelomus restates his prefatory programme: first lay the foundations of history, then raise the summit of allegory or spiritual understanding, inserting moral harmony where fitting. He then begins the historical exposition of Elcana's genealogy and promises a spiritual reading later.

author: Angelomus Luxovensis
title: Enarrationes in libros Regum (Angelomus Luxovensis)
example_figure: classis Salomonis in Ophir; aurum quadringentorum viginti talentorum
summary: Solomon's fleet sailing to Ophir is read as the Church's learned (Jew and Gentile) seeking the precious sense beneath the letter. The gold brought back is the history expounded allegorically and tropologically, with anagoge found in both Testaments.

author: Haymo Halberstatensis
title: Commentarium in Cantica canticorum (Haymo Halberstatensis)
senses_latin: intelligentia spiritualis > littera > allegoria > moralitas > anagoge
definitions: anagoge: the higher sense | intelligentia spiritualis: spiritual meaning contained within the letter, like honey in the wax
summary: Commenting on the dripping honeycomb (honey in wax = spiritual meaning in the letter), Haymo says Scripture overflows because it is understood in many senses: literal, allegorical, moral and anagogical, the last glossed as the higher sense.

author: Paulus Alvarus Cordubensis
title: Epistolae (Paulus Alvarus Cordubensis)
senses_latin: historialiter > moraliter > active > mysticum > spiritale > allegoria
example_figure: columba deargentata, dorsum in pallore auri
summary: The dove of Ps 67 is the Holy Spirit and figures Scripture. Its silver wings are whatever Scripture holds historically, morally and actively, open to all readers. Its golden back is the mystical, spiritual, allegorical sense, hidden for the wise. Scripture is body and spirit.

author: Hincmarus Rhemensis
title: De verbis Psalmi (Hincmarus Rhemensis)
senses_latin: littera > typicus > moralis intelligentia > mysticus sensus
example_figure: fulica et herodius; cedri Libani; passeres
summary: Hincmar says he has written on the coot and heron according to the letter, from great authors. He declines to expound the typical or moral sense at length, but briefly signifies the mystical sense of Ps 103: cedars as nobles, sparrows as the humble.

author: Notkerus Balbulus
title: De interpretibus divinarum Scripturarum (Notkerus Balbulus)
summary: Notker's bibliographic guide says Gregory's commentary on Job built morality on the foundation of history and crowned it with the roof of anagoge. It then notes that Bede tried to turn the simple history of Tobit and Ezra into allegory.

author: Notkerus Balbulus
title: De interpretibus divinarum Scripturarum (Notkerus Balbulus)
summary: Notker recommends Prosper's De promissis et praedictis Dei as a rule for all scripture, distinguishing what happened only historically, what happened historically but signifies morally or anagogically, and what is merely future or promised.

author: Odo Cluniacensis
title: Moralia in Job (Odo Cluniacensis)
senses_latin: moralis > allegoricus > typicus > tropicus > mysticus > litteralis > historicus > parabolicus > tropologicus > etymologicus > anagogicus > analogicus > exemplaris > anaphoricus > proportionalis > apocalypticus > boarcademicus > primordialis
definitions: allegoria: a sustained, continued parable: one thing is said, another understood
summary: Editor's preface to Odo's Moralia in Job: the Church teaches through several senses. It lists eight senses, each with a paired alternative name, and proposes to prove them from Gal 4:24. Literal and allegorical are derived there, allegory defined.

author: Odo Cluniacensis
title: Moralia in Job (Odo Cluniacensis)
senses_latin: typicus > exemplaris > anaphoricus > proportionalis > mysticus > apocalypticus > boarcademicus > primordialis > litteralis > allegoricus > tropologicus > anagogicus
example_figure: Abraham et duo filii (Isaac et Ismael)
definitions: allegoria: a sustained, continuous parable: one thing is said, another understood | tropologia: moral comparison of past deeds to our own times, so that we act likewise; discourse on morals | anagogicus: sense leading back from earthly things to heavenly | typicus: one person standing for and representing another person
summary: Lists an extended scheme of senses (literal, allegorical, tropological, anagogical, typical, anaphoric, mystical, boarcademic) and derives each from Gal 4 (Abraham's two sons). It defines allegory, tropology, anagogy and the typical sense, confirming each with other scriptural texts.

author: Odo Cluniacensis
title: Moralia in Job (Odo Cluniacensis)
senses_latin: boarcademicus > litteralis > allegoricus > tropologicus > anagogicus > typicus > anaphoricus > mysticus
authority: Hieronymus, Gregorius, Ambrosius, Augustinus, Basilius, Bernardus, Clemens, Nazianzenus
definitions: boarcademicus: the principles of things compared with eternal beatitude and the whole economy of salvation
summary: End of an extended scheme of senses, evidently a later editorial note since it cites Bernard. It defines a final cabbalistic 'boarcademicus' sense, proved from 4 Ezra, then assigns literal, allegorical, tropological, anagogical, typical, anaphoric and mystical senses to particular doctors.

author: Atto Vercellensis
title: Expositio epistolarum S. Pauli (Atto Vercellensis)
summary: Commenting on 2 Cor 3, Atto says some parts of the law must be read only as written. Allegorizing the Decalogue opens the door to vice by destroying moral progress. Other parts are read only historically, others both ways; either way the law is superseded by grace.
